A few days ago, I walked along a quiet stretch at West Point overlooking the Hudson River — where the granite walls of the Academy meet the turning leaves of fall. Along the path, a series of black stone plaques tell the story of a nation that once tore itself apart — and then, slowly, found its way back together.
Each stone marks a moment between 1861 and 1913, a span that begins with division and ends with reunion. Together, they tell a story we desperately need to remember.
The Cost of Division
During the Civil War, West Point graduates fought on both sides. Brothers-in-arms became enemies overnight. In one of the plaques, General Ulysses S. Grant — Class of 1843 — said in 1861,
“There are but two parties now, traitors and patriots, and I want hereafter to be ranked with the latter.”
At the time, the divide felt absolute. But Grant’s words weren’t born of hatred — they were born of duty. And duty, at West Point, is never about self. It’s about country.
Today, our divides aren’t drawn in gray and blue, but they are real. We live in an era of polarization where we too often mistake our political opponents for enemies. The lesson from those years is simple and sobering: division is easy; reconciliation takes courage.
Humanity Amid Conflict
Another plaque tells the story of Gettysburg, July 3, 1863. Confederate General Lewis Armistead, mortally wounded during Pickett’s Charge, gasped his last words to Union officers:
“Tell Hancock I have done him and my country a great injustice which I shall never cease to regret.”
Hancock — his old West Point friend — was fighting for the Union. Even in his final moments, Armistead recognized that friendship and conscience transcend ideology.
That’s a lesson for our own time. We can disagree without dehumanizing. We can hold convictions without surrendering compassion. The humanity that binds us is more powerful than the politics that divide us.
Lincoln’s Call for Mercy
In March 1865, as the war neared its end, Abraham Lincoln stood on the Capitol steps and offered a moral vision that still shines:
“With malice toward none, with charity for all… to bind up the nation’s wounds.”
Lincoln’s words weren’t naïve. He had seen the blood and bitterness of war firsthand. His greatness lay in his ability to forgive without forgetting — to choose mercy when vengeance was easier.
That’s leadership. That’s strength.
In today’s political culture, outrage is rewarded and grace is rare. But if we want to preserve this fragile experiment in self-government, we must recover Lincoln’s courage — not just to fight for what’s right, but to heal what’s broken.
Grant and Lee: Dignity in Defeat
At Appomattox Court House, two West Point men — Grant and Lee — met to end the war. Grant offered generous terms to the Confederate soldiers: they could return home, keep their horses, and rebuild. Lee responded,
“This will have the best possible effect upon the men… it will do much toward conciliating our people.”
Imagine that. Two generals, both hardened by years of war, still understood that peace required humility and respect.
Leadership isn’t about victory at all costs. It’s about knowing when to stop fighting, when to show grace, and when to lift others up so the nation can move forward together.
From Division to Reunion
After the war, former West Point cadets began to meet again. They created the Association of Graduates in 1869 “to perpetuate friendships” and “to promote the best interests of the Academy.”
By 1902, at West Point’s Centennial, and 1913, at Gettysburg’s 50th Anniversary, veterans from both sides stood side by side — not as Union or Confederate, but as Americans.
The plaques record their words:
“We meet on this occasion to participate in a ceremony that stands unmatched in history, for nowhere in history have men who opposed each other in mighty battle come together in peace.”
Half a century earlier, they had fought to the death. Now, they shook hands.
“Let Us Have Peace”-read

What a cold review. Israel is a very young country under constant wars. I don’t disagree with some of the details, but Jerusalem has so much to offer some of the most stunning places on earth, and each stone tells a story. More and more haredim serve in the army, many of them are very successful. Israelis are not fake-nice like Americans who smile and greet you but won’t help in times of need. They unite and will die for their neighbors. We don’t stand in lines in Israel (I do it in America and elsewhere) and we push we’re Middle Eastern by nature, lol but we do it with love not hatred. 

If you come with a patronizing attitude, you’ll never enjoy it. Come humble and understanding, and you’ll fall in love. Israel is not for the faint of heart and weak it’s for those who can see through the dust and recognize an eternal potential and purpose, which is why the most successful people in the world invest in and believe in Israel. Israel is not what you see in the streets. Israel is what is inside the heart and soul of the people.

text:
Jerusalem was an interesting city.  I didn’t find it “magical” and none of the so called Holy sites had much of an impact on me (I suppose I’m more Greek than I thought) but one angle you cannot deny is that there’s a certain vitality to the city, youth, young children everywhere.  Even late into the night on a weekday.  Food was good.  Often quite good.  Much more expensive than I had assumed though.  Beer selection was terrible, but that’s to be expected.  Interesting dynamic: young and attractive European looking women with very homely men.  Also Israelis love their sweets.  It seemed like every other shop was selling some sort of sugar bread.  The orange juice was excellent.  

Re: youth:.  Are they just 30-40 years behind us, demographically? I’m not sure.  But most of the fecundity seemed to be concentrated in the Haredi community - a group who don’t work and don’t fight in the IDF.  Something like 15-20 percent of the population and rising rapidly. From an outsider, appeared like a ticking time bomb. In the early mornings the IDF conscripts were close to my hotel using public transit to commute to base - it looked nothing like the slop the boomers post on Facebook.  The majority seemed either Mizrahi or some sort of African.  A small sample size though.  

The city itself seemed like a mixture of both Europe and the Middle East (I was not in Tel Aviv, just in and around Jerusalem). People were mostly cold and standoffish.  Nobody queues at the tram and bus stops.  Shoving and cutting in is the name of the game.  A cashier at the supermarket gave me 50 shekels in change when she realized I didn’t speak Hebrew (I watched her count it out- this was clearly an insult) -had some haredi kids come up to me and ask me to buy their meal for them (I obviously said no).  The train system was lovely and the entire country seemed to be under construction - high rise towers popping up everywhere.  Gas seemed at least 50% higher than the US.  New real estate developments were nice, but quite expensive.  

I’ll have some thoughts later on NatCon (perhaps) but just wanted give a quick review of the city as my memory still works.

text:
My friend Dapo kept two things in his wardrobe: a flight confirmation from the agent and an offer letter from the man who used to be his boss.

For three years, the ticket had been his whole prayer. The letter had only been there nine days.
"Stay," his wife, Yemisi, said, scraping the last of the rice into their children's plates. "Abroad will not be a joke. I don't want to hear you've become somebody's night cleaner."

"Go," said his friend Gbenga on the phone. "Naira is falling like it has no brakes. Two years from now, that salary will buy you pure water."
Dapo said "Hmm" to both of them. It was the only word he had left.
On Saturday, he took his eldest, Kemi, on his motorbike to the market. She was nine and noticed everything.

At a roadside stall, an old man was selling second-hand shoes. Kemi stopped and pointed at a pair with a broken strap.

"Daddy, why is he smiling? These ones are spoilt."
"Maybe he fixes them."
"But if he fixes them, will they still carry people?"
Dapo laughed. Then he stopped laughing.

That night, he lay awake while the generator coughed outside. In his head he did the sums again: the ₦9 million, the car, the commission, the snow, the plates. Every road ended with a question he couldn't answer.

At 3 a.m., he went to the sitting room and found Yemisi already there in the dark, a wrapper tied over her nightdress.

"I'm not sleeping either," she said. "I said stay because I'm afraid. Not because I'm sure."

"I said go because I'm tired," he admitted. "Not because I'm brave."
They sat there for a while, two frightened people holding the same fear from opposite ends.

In the morning, Yemisi found a page torn from Kemi's exercise book on the dining table. In careful pencil, her daughter had drawn a house, a plane, and a car, all connected by one long road.

Underneath she had written: Daddy, wherever the road goes, we are in the car.
Dapo stood there reading it with his tea going cold.

He didn't decide that morning. But for the first time in weeks, he stopped asking which one, and started asking how, together.
Some choices aren't between staying and leaving. They're about who sits in the car with you.

text:
As our Cambodian friends celebrate the Pchum Ben, families make their way to pagodas with food, prayers and offerings to honour their departed ancestors.

Among the foods prepared for the occasion is Bay Ben—small balls of sticky rice. Some are offered at the pagoda, while others are traditionally scattered around the temple grounds or nearby fields.

The practice is connected to the belief that wandering or suffering spirits may be unable to enter sacred places. By leaving Bay Ben outside, families ensure that these spirits are not left without food as they remember those who have passed before them.

It is one of the traditions that marks Pchum Ben, bringing together remembrance, family and Buddhist practice in Cambodia.

text:
The importance of Duffy's testimony was limited to whether his particular injury could have produced the marks. His denial did not independently identify the stains as Mary Phagan's blood (State of Georgia v. Frank, 15).

April 23, 1914: Waggoner and Doral investigate Duffy

The Georgia Supreme Court appeal record preserves a joint sworn statement attributed to Robert L. Waggoner and Detective J. H. Doral.

The statement appears on pages 1644–1645 of the appellate record.

The detectives identified themselves as members of the Atlanta Police Department and stated that they were acquainted with Duffy.

They described an earlier conversation with him at police headquarters concerning the injury to his hand.

According to Waggoner and Doral, Duffy had firmly rejected the suggestion that blood from his wounded finger could explain the disputed factory stains.

The detectives reported that Duffy had already been holding cotton waste when the injury occurred and had immediately wrapped it around the wounded finger.

They attributed to Duffy the explanation that he held the wound tightly while leaving the work area and proceeding toward Frank's office.

The account supported Duffy's original trial testimony and challenged the later suggestion that considerable blood from the accident might have reached the dressing-room area.

Waggoner and Doral were not eyewitnesses to the industrial accident. Their testimony concerned statements allegedly made by Duffy during the investigation.

Their evidence therefore addressed the credibility and consistency of Duffy's explanations (Georgia Supreme Court Appeal Record, 1) (Georgia Supreme Court Appeal Record, 16).

The question of witness compensation

The detectives also described visiting Duffy at his Atlanta home on Thursday evening, April 23, 1914.

According to their account, Duffy said Solicitor Dorsey had approved his witness subpoena, permitting him to obtain compensation from the county treasurer.

The amount discussed was approximately $7.50.

The appeal record also contains a statement from Fulton County Treasurer H. L. Culerson describing a witness payment of $7.60 during August 1913.

The record contains inconsistencies in the initials assigned to Duffy in the compensation material, requiring care when identifying the exact payee.

The State used the explanation concerning ordinary witness fees while disputing allegations of improper payments associated with testimony.

Waggoner's involvement consequently concerned both Duffy's explanation of the bloodstains and the circumstances surrounding his earlier appearance as a prosecution witness (Georgia Supreme Court Appeal Record, 16).

May 3, 1914: Duffy's conflicting affidavits

The controversy became more complicated during the proceedings over Frank's extraordinary motion for a new trial.

The defense presented an affidavit in which Duffy questioned his original testimony and suggested that more blood might have fallen from his wounded hand than he had acknowledged in court.

He also complained about the manner in which Solicitor Dorsey had questioned him.

A few weeks later, Duffy changed his account again.

The Atlanta Journal of Sunday, May 3, 1914, page 33, column 4, reported that Duffy had been arrested on a court attachment on Friday night, May 1, and remained detained during Saturday.

He then signed another affidavit reaffirming his original testimony and accusing representatives associated with the defense of bribing him to change his account.

The accusations were contested.

These competing statements created serious questions about Duffy's reliability and the circumstances under which the affidavits had been obtained.

Waggoner's sworn statement belonged to the State's effort to challenge the defense's new account and preserve the credibility of Duffy's earlier explanation.

This episode is historically important, but the chronology must remain clear.

Duffy's original account was heard during Frank's trial in August 1913. Waggoner's testimony concerning Duffy emerged during the 1914 appellate proceedings.

The latter could influence the legal contest over the conviction, but it was not evidence considered by the original jury (Atlanta Journal, 17).

October 1913: The Ira Fisher investigation

Between the verdict and the Duffy controversy, Waggoner was involved in another development concerning the Frank case.

During October 19–20, 1913, Frank's attorneys investigated statements made by Ira W. Fisher, who had accused another individual of involvement in Mary Phagan's murder.

The Atlanta Constitution identified Waggoner, Coker, Garner, and Detective John N. Starnes among the officers seeking to investigate Fisher's allegations.

The matter produced a disagreement between the detective department and Frank's attorneys, Luther Rosser and Reuben Arnold.

Rosser wanted police cooperation in examining Fisher's information. The detectives insisted upon conducting their inquiries according to their own judgment.

The contemporary accounts show that Waggoner remained involved in developments surrounding the case approximately eight weeks after Frank's conviction.

The newspaper reports document his participation in investigating the allegations, without establishing the truth of Fisher's alternative account (Atlanta Constitution, 18).

August 4, 1913: A photograph of Detective Waggoner

A contemporary photograph of Waggoner appeared in The Atlanta Constitution on Monday, August 4, 1913, page 1, column 5.

The illustrated feature was headed:

"Their Testimony Is Important in the Trial of Leo M. Frank."

It contained photographs of Emil Selig, Detective Waggoner, Dr. H. F. Harris, and Chief of Detectives Newport A. Lanford.

The photographs were credited to staff photographer Francis E. Price.

The detective's caption mistakenly gave his initials as D. L., but the accompanying text identified him as the detective who had testified on Saturday morning.

The photograph provides a contemporary visual record of Waggoner during the trial and offers a useful illustration for his biography (Atlanta Constitution, 19).

1916–1919: A supervisory career in Atlanta policing

Waggoner remained with the Atlanta Police Department following the Frank proceedings.

On Sunday, April 2, 1916, The Atlanta Constitution reported that Chief of Detectives Newport Lanford was ill and confined to his home.

During Lanford's absence, Detective Sergeant Bob Waggoner was placed temporarily in charge of the detective department.

His appointment establishes that he had advanced to a position of supervisory responsibility.

In May 1918, Waggoner testified during an Atlanta City Council investigation concerning police practices.

The Atlanta Georgian reported his statements about the distribution of alcoholic beverages seized during police raids.

Waggoner acknowledged distributing confiscated liquor to police personnel and public officials, frequently under instructions from Lanford.

The proceedings exposed considerable disagreement within the police department. They do not establish a criminal conviction against Waggoner (Atlanta Georgian, 20).

By Wednesday, September 17, 1919, The Atlanta Georgian identified Bob Waggoner as a lieutenant of detectives.

The newspaper described his participation, along with Detectives Jamison, Brown, and Doyal, in apprehending two men suspected of attempting to rob a store near North Boulevard and Tenth Street.

This report extends his documented professional advancement beyond the sergeant rank recorded in the 1919 city directory.

His police career therefore continued for at least six years following the Phagan murder trial, with newspaper evidence of responsibility for both supervisory duties and ordinary criminal investigations (Atlanta Georgian, 21).

The genealogical record and his unidentified final years

The available directories and newspapers establish a working biography of Robert L. Waggoner.

He was living in Atlanta by 1906, was married to Mattie, and worked in the city's electric street railway system.

Around 1909, he entered law enforcement. By 1913, he was serving as a city detective.

He resided at 53 South Jackson Street during 1906 and 1909 and at 86 Waddell Street from at least 1912 through 1919.

His documented ranks included detective, detective sergeant, and lieutenant of detectives.

The legal records establish his full first name as Robert, while the contemporary newspaper photograph provides a visual identification.

His parents, exact birth date, middle name, wife's maiden name, children, date of death, and burial place remain unidentified in the verified material.

The strongest genealogical leads are his Atlanta addresses and the federal census records covering the surrounding years.

Original police personnel files, pension records, marriage certificates, and death records may provide the remaining details.

Conclusion: Waggoner's place in the evidence against Leo Frank

Robert L. Waggoner occupied a relatively small but identifiable place in the prosecution of Leo M. Frank.

His importance at the original trial arose from his observations of the superintendent on Tuesday, April 29, 1913.

Waggoner described repeated approaches to an office window, twisting of hands, and trembling during an automobile journey to police headquarters.

These observations supported Dorsey's argument concerning Frank's consciousness of guilt.

The trial brief and three contemporary newspapers agree on the essential actions while differing over such details as the automobile seating arrangement, the identity of other persons in the office, and Frank's formal arrest status.

The newspaper accounts also preserve courtroom exchanges missing from the condensed legal brief, including Waggoner's estimate of fifty feet from the window and his demonstration of trembling.

Dorsey's August 25 closing argument establishes that the detective's testimony was intentionally incorporated into the State's final presentation.

The later appellate statement concerning J. E. Duffy identifies Waggoner with another important dispute, the possibility that an employee's wounded hand explained the suspected bloodstains near the second-floor dressing room.

His 1914 statement challenged an alternative explanation for those marks and supported Duffy's original trial account.

Neither role made Waggoner an eyewitness to Mary Phagan's murder. His original evidence concerned events three days after the crime, while his later statement concerned conversations about an earlier industrial accident.

The detective's testimony must therefore be understood as circumstantial evidence. It acquired significance from its relationship to other testimony and the conclusions urged by the prosecution.

Waggoner's biography also reveals a career extending well beyond the murder investigation. From an electric streetcar employee in 1906, he rose through the Atlanta detective department and eventually held the rank of lieutenant.

His surviving testimony, legal statements, newspaper coverage, city directory entries, and contemporary photograph establish his place in both the Leo Frank case and Atlanta's early twentieth-century police history.

🏈 SUNDAY NFL FREE PICKS — OCTOBER 11

🔥 FREE PLAY — NEW ORLEANS +2.5 over MINNESOTA — 1:00 ET

Minnesota's undefeated record is impressive, but the Vikings' underlying performance tells a substantially different story. Their defense has been outstanding, while their offense has struggled to produce even against vulnerable opponents.

Minnesota is averaging only 4.4 yards per offensive play and has managed just one touchdown over its last three games. That is an extraordinary lack of offensive production for an undefeated team, particularly one being asked to lay points on the road.

Quarterback Kyler Murray has struggled to generate consistent downfield production, forcing the Vikings to rely heavily on defensive stops and field goals. Minnesota's inability to finish drives creates a legitimate concern when laying points against a home opponent.

The Luck Factor provides one of the strongest regression indicators on the NFL board. Minnesota is +1.6 wins above expectation, while New Orleans is -0.6. That creates a 2.2-win gap favoring positive regression toward the Saints. After only four games, that discrepancy is substantial, although it should not be mechanically converted into points.

The market also presents an attractive contrarian opportunity. Minnesota's perfect record and elite defensive statistics have attracted considerable public support. New Orleans receives corroborated worldwide contrarian support against a popular road favorite.

A respected sharp bettor independently supports the Saints, having established a position when New Orleans was receiving fewer points. That provides additional confirmation that the available +2.5 offers value.

Minnesota's defense is unquestionably capable of dominating stretches of this matchup. However, the Vikings' offensive limitations make it difficult to justify their favorite status, especially away from home.

New Orleans has the offensive capability to challenge Minnesota more effectively than the Vikings' recent opponents, and the Saints do not need to win outright to reward their backers.

Play to: NEW ORLEANS +2.5.

🔥 FREE PLAY — NY JETS -2.5 over CLEVELAND — 1:00 ET

This is one of the strongest corroborated worldwide contrarian opportunities of the NFL weekend.

Cleveland is receiving overwhelming public support despite being a road underdog. Across multiple betting markets, the Browns have attracted a remarkably large share of spread selections. Our worldwide contrarian indexes, incorporating legal U.S. markets, Las Vegas, offshore activity and additional market intelligence, strongly support taking the opposite side.

Public underdogs are especially important in our methodology. When bettors overwhelmingly support a team receiving points, it often reflects excessive confidence in that team's recent results rather than an accurate assessment of the underlying matchup.

Cleveland's record provides an excellent example.

The Browns have benefited from unusually favorable outcomes relative to their underlying performance. Their Luck Factor stands at +1.6, indicating that their actual victories have exceeded expectation.

The Jets are at -0.4, creating a 2.0-win regression gap favoring New York. That is one of the largest discrepancies among Sunday's matchups and suggests the market may be overvaluing Cleveland's results while discounting the Jets.

The Browns' defense could also be weakened by the expected absence of defensive lineman Mason Graham. His ability to disrupt the interior offensive line is particularly important against a quarterback who benefits from a clean pocket. Removing that pressure threat could improve New York's opportunities to sustain drives and finish possessions.

Cleveland has demonstrated offensive improvement, including a productive performance against Pittsburgh. That is a legitimate concern, especially because New York's defense endured an unusually demanding workload against Chicago.

Nevertheless, the combination of substantial worldwide contrarian support, an exceptional Luck Factor discrepancy and the potential Cleveland defensive personnel loss creates a compelling case for the home favorite.

The spread is another important consideration. New York needs to win by only a field goal to cover -2.5, preserving the value of the NFL's most important scoring margin.

Play to: NY JETS -2.5.

🔥 FREE PLAY — WASHINGTON -3.5 over NY GIANTS — 1:00 ET

Washington qualifies as another powerful worldwide contrarian selection, with the public heavily supporting the Giants despite their status as road underdogs.

Multiple independent betting samples show substantial ticket support for New York. That is precisely the type of market imbalance receiving additional weight in our methodology: bettors taking points with an underdog whose recent results have created an inflated perception of its true strength.

The Giants' record has been considerably better than their underlying performance suggests.

New York's Luck Factor is +0.9, while Washington stands at -0.4. That produces a 1.3-win regression advantage toward the Commanders.

The distinction matters because the market frequently responds to wins and losses more strongly than to the quality of the performances producing those results. A team benefiting from favorable variance can appear stronger than it actually is, particularly early in the season.

Washington has experienced the opposite situation. Its actual results have undersold its underlying performance, creating an opportunity for the market to underestimate the Commanders.

The matchup also favors Washington from a situational standpoint. Playing at home against a division opponent, the Commanders have an opportunity to dictate offensive tempo and place pressure on a Giants team whose results have been supported by favorable variance.

The biggest consideration is the spread. Washington is laying more than a field goal, and that additional half-point matters considerably in the NFL. A three-point Washington victory would not be enough.

However, the strength of the worldwide contrarian agreement and the underlying regression discrepancy provide enough support to back the favorite at the available number.

Play to: WASHINGTON -3.5.

🔥 FREE PLAY — LAS VEGAS +3.5 over NEW ENGLAND — 1:00 ET

Las Vegas presents an intriguing combination of professional support, situational value and an attractive spread.

The Raiders have shown considerably more competitiveness than their reputation suggests. In their most recent divisional matchup, Las Vegas remained competitive for much of the game before a costly special-teams mistake contributed to the defeat.

That result is important because the final score does not fully reflect how closely the Raiders competed.

New England enters following an emotional road victory over Buffalo. Beating a major division rival can create a difficult motivational and preparation situation the following week, particularly when the market responds by upgrading the winning team's perceived strength.

Las Vegas faces the opposite circumstances. Coming off a frustrating divisional defeat, the Raiders have a clear opportunity to respond against an opponent receiving considerable attention for its previous victory.

A respected sharp bettor independently supports Las Vegas +3.5 and projects New England as approximately a two-point favorite. That creates meaningful separation between the professional assessment and the available market number.

The key is receiving more than a field goal. A three-point New England victory still produces a winning ticket on Las Vegas.

The Luck Factor does not strengthen the Raiders' case. Las Vegas is +0.8 compared with New England's +0.3, indicating that the Raiders have actually benefited from somewhat more favorable variance. That makes the professional matchup assessment and available price particularly important.

The Patriots possess offensive matchup advantages, especially in the running game, but those advantages must be weighed against the difficulty of laying more than a field goal against a competitive opponent.

The situational setup, professional support and valuable half-point beyond three provide the strongest arguments for Las Vegas.

Play to: LAS VEGAS +3.5.

🔥 FREE PLAY — UNDER 42.5 MINNESOTA/NEW ORLEANS — 1:00 ET

Minnesota has one of the NFL's most unusual early-season profiles: an undefeated team supported by an elite defense and an offense that has struggled to score touchdowns.

The Vikings rank first in defensive EPA per play, defensive success rate and scoring defense. Those are meaningful efficiency measurements because they evaluate how consistently a defense prevents productive plays rather than simply counting points allowed.

Minnesota's defense has repeatedly forced opponents into difficult down-and-distance situations, limiting sustained possessions and making explosive scoring drives difficult to produce.

Offensively, however, the Vikings have been among the least productive teams in football.

Minnesota is averaging only 4.4 yards per play and has scored one offensive touchdown over its last three games. Even when the Vikings have moved the ball into scoring position, they have frequently settled for field goals.

That inability to finish drives is particularly important for a total of 42.5. Sustained possessions ending in three points rather than seven can dramatically reduce the final score.

Quarterback Kyler Murray has not consistently generated the explosive passing production necessary to overcome those offensive limitations.

New Orleans faces the difficult assignment of attacking the league's most efficient defense. The Saints may find opportunities in the running game, but consistently finishing drives against Minnesota remains a substantial challenge.

The expected game script favors controlled possessions, defensive stops and limited explosive plays rather than a high-scoring exchange.

A respected sharp bettor independently supports the UNDER at 42.5, providing professional corroboration for the defensive and offensive efficiency analysis.

This selection is based on projected possessions, scoring efficiency and matchup characteristics. Win-based Luck Factor is excluded from totals.

Play to: UNDER 42.5.

🔥 FREE PLAY — OVER 39.5 CLEVELAND/NY JETS — 1:00 ET

Cleveland's offensive improvement creates an opportunity against a Jets defense facing a difficult recovery situation.

The Browns have become progressively more productive since their opening game. Their most recent performance included 27 points against Pittsburgh, with three touchdowns coming in the first half.

That production is particularly meaningful because Cleveland demonstrated the ability to sustain drives and finish possessions against a respectable defensive opponent.

The Browns now face a New York defense coming off one of the NFL's most demanding recent workloads.

Chicago ran 89 offensive plays against the Jets and possessed the football for nearly 43 minutes. That left New York's defense on the field for an extraordinary portion of the game.

Such an imbalance can affect defensive recovery, particularly when players are repeatedly forced to tackle, defend extended possessions and maintain their assignments while fatigued.

Cleveland also benefits from additional preparation and recovery time following its Thursday game. That scheduling advantage provides an opportunity to develop a more effective offensive plan against New York's defensive weaknesses.

The Jets have scoring opportunities of their own.

Cleveland defensive lineman Mason Graham is expected to miss the game, potentially reducing the Browns' interior pressure and improving New York's ability to protect quarterback Geno Smith.

That is important because the OVER does not require Cleveland to dominate offensively. Contributions from both teams create multiple paths to exceeding a relatively modest total.

Professional support is particularly noteworthy. A respected sharp bettor backs the full-game OVER and has made a substantially larger commitment to Cleveland exceeding 18.5 team points.

Those positions are related rather than independent, but they reinforce the expectation that Cleveland can produce meaningful offensive scoring.

The independent matchup assessment places the appropriate total closer to 41 points. The estimated advantage is modest, but the combination of Cleveland's offensive improvement, New York's defensive workload and the personnel situation supports the higher-scoring outcome.

Play to: OVER 39.5.

🔥 FREE PLAY — UNDER 42.5 DENVER/LA CHARGERS — 4:05 ET

Both offenses face significant obstacles to consistent scoring, creating a compelling case for the UNDER in this AFC West matchup.

Denver has struggled to generate explosive passing plays, particularly away from home. The Broncos' passing attack has repeatedly relied on short throws that produce limited yardage after the catch.

That approach creates problems when an offense must sustain long drives without the benefit of explosive gains.

Even when Denver moves the chains, the lack of downfield production increases the number of successful plays required to reach scoring position. More plays create additional opportunities for sacks, penalties, incompletions and stalled possessions.

The Chargers face a different but equally significant problem.

Los Angeles has been dealing with injuries to both starting offensive tackles. Those absences can materially affect pass protection, especially against a Denver defense capable of generating pressure from multiple alignments.

When offensive tackles are unavailable, teams often compensate by keeping tight ends or running backs in protection. That reduces the number of eligible receivers available downfield and can force quarterbacks into quicker, shorter passing concepts.

The consequences extend beyond sacks. Pressure can disrupt timing, eliminate deep passing opportunities and make third-down conversions considerably more difficult.

Denver's defensive front has the personnel to exploit those weaknesses, while the Broncos' own offensive limitations make it difficult to project consistent scoring from the other side.

A respected sharp bettor independently supports the UNDER at 42.5.

The matchup points toward reduced passing efficiency, fewer explosive gains and more possessions ending without touchdowns. Those factors provide a stronger foundation for the UNDER than simply relying on either team's recent scoring averages.

Play to: UNDER 42.5.

“Free Palestine” from what, exactly?
Israel completely withdrew from Gaza in 2005—every soldier, every civilian, even the graves. Palestinians had a chance to build something. Instead Hamas took over in 2007, canceled elections, and spent the next 16 years turning aid and cement into rockets and a massive tunnel network while keeping Gaza as a launchpad against Israel.
Palestinian leadership has rejected multiple offers of statehood (Camp David 2000, Clinton parameters, Olmert’s 2008 offer of nearly the entire West Bank with land swaps and shared Jerusalem). The consistent demand has been “from the river to the sea”—no Jewish state at all. That’s why the PLO’s original charter predated the 1967 lines.

text:
Seems like you’re only looking at one side of the equation. You’re focused on the leverage players lose after transferring while ignoring how the financial incentives change before they ever enter the portal.

Using Altmyer at Ole Miss as an example. Completely hypothetical numbers, but say Ole Miss offers him $500k to stay as a backup while Illinois offers $500k with a clear path to starting. Obviously, transferring makes a ton of sense under the current system.

Now imagine under the proposed rules Ole Miss can offer him $1.5M to stay because it has access to the new $22.5M retention pool that Illinois can’t use to recruit him. Illinois is still offering $500k. Suddenly that’s a much tougher decision. He might never enter the portal to begin with.

And if he still transfers to Illinois and breaks out, we’d have access to that same retention pool after his first season to increase his comp. Why would Illinois pay him more? Because keeping a proven starting QB still has tremendous value and if you don’t then other teams can call that out to try to spook future transfers from signing with you. You don’t want the reputation as the team who doesn’t pay transfers after they’ve proven themselves as contributors.

You’re right that players who’ve already transferred would have less negotiating leverage…that’s a fair criticism. Just don’t think it’s as substantial of a loss as you’re making it out to be. Especially because the bill could make staying at your current school substantially more financially attractive than exploring the portal in the first place.

text:
Daily Word of God

The Widow’s Mite

Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury. - Mark 12:43 (BSB)

It’s important to pay attention to how our Lord values the gifts we offer. Just as He saw the offerings made at the temple that day and spoke about their worth, He still watches how we give and measures our gifts in the same way. It’s encouraging to know that the size of our offerings doesn’t determine their greatness or acceptance in heaven’s sight. The widow’s mite outweighed the rich man’s large contribution.

No doubt this poor woman felt her gift was so small that it barely seemed worth giving, but in the eyes of the Lord, its value was immense. There are two scales that weigh human acts and gifts. There are earthly scales, which measure in terms of money and possessions, and there are heavenly scales that weigh spiritual value. In the heavenly scales, the widow’s mites weighed more than the rich man’s coins, given with such display.

This wasn’t just because her gift was proportionally larger—she gave all she had, while the rich still had much left—but also because of her motive and spirit. She gave out of love for God and a desire to support His house, not to be seen by others. Her offering was humble and sincere, given to honor God. Her gift was large in proportion to her ability, putting the rich to shame for giving so much while still keeping so much more for themselves. Christ looks at the heart when we give, and if our hearts are right and we give out of love for God, even the smallest offering is pleasing to Him and will receive heaven’s commendation. In heaven, gifts are not measured by dollars and cents, and many large gifts may turn out to be very small in the heavenly balance.

text:
Beloved brethren in the Lord, as the shadows of evening lengthen and we turn our hearts toward prayer in this quiet hour, let us meditate upon the sacred words from the first book of Maccabees: "...they offered praise and thanksgiving... with gladness." In the year 164 before the coming of our Savior, the valiant Judas Maccabeus, raised up by divine providence amid the tyranny of Antiochus Epiphanes, purified the desecrated Temple in Jerusalem. The altar, once profaned by pagan abominations, was renewed with fresh stones, the sacred vessels restored, and the people gathered to offer holocausts, singing hymns of joy as the light of the menorah once more illumined the holy place. This act of rededication, born from faithful resistance and trust in the Most High, birthed the feast that echoes still in the memory of God's people.

The early fathers, those luminous voices of the apostolic age, discerned in these events a profound foreshadowing of the spiritual temple within each soul. St. Augustine, in his homilies on the Psalms, teaches that such gladness is no mere emotion but the fruit of the Spirit, arising when the heart, cleansed of idols, offers the true sacrifice of praise. Origen and St. Jerome, commenting on the Maccabean struggles, saw here the pattern of the Church's own purification through persecution, where thanksgiving becomes the weapon against despair. The Catena Aurea gathers these insights, reminding us that the joy of the Maccabees prefigures the resurrection gladness of the apostles, a rejoicing not in earthly victory but in the Lord's abiding presence. Historically, this dedication parallels Solomon's temple consecration and the return from Babylonian exile, each marked by communal worship that unites past deliverance with present hope.

Therefore, my children, in the stillness of this evening, let us restore the altars of our own hearts. Offer praise and thanksgiving with gladness, for the Lord has consecrated us through the eternal sacrifice of His Son. As the blessed Chrysostom exhorts in his discourses on worship, let not trials silence your song, but let gratitude rise like incense, transforming every burden into an occasion for deeper faith. The Church, the new Israel, continues this sacred tradition in her liturgies, where evening prayer echoes the Maccabean hymns. May this verse awaken in you an unquenchable spirit of joy, leading all to the eternal temple of heaven.

text:
🚨💔 HE SPENT 180 DAYS GETTING READY TO CHANGE HIS LIFE. HIS BEST FRIEND STARTED IN JUST SIX DAYS. SIX MONTHS LATER, ONE HAD A PERFECT PLAN. THE OTHER HAD A STORY THAT WOULD CHANGE EVERYTHING.

But what happened when they met again was something neither of them expected.

One man had spent six months studying, researching, planning, and preparing.

The other had spent six months making mistakes, facing rejection, losing confidence, finding solutions, and slowly building something real.

One knew almost everything about starting a business.

The other had actually started one.

And when the first man finally asked his friend how he'd managed to get so far, the answer nearly brought him to tears.

"BECAUSE I WAS WILLING TO LOOK STUPID FOR SIX MONTHS WHILE YOU WERE TRYING TO LOOK SMART."

Those words hurt.

Not because they were intended to be cruel.

But because they exposed something he'd been hiding from himself.

For six months, he'd told his wife he was working toward a better future.

For six months, he'd sacrificed evenings with his children.

For six months, he'd stayed awake until 2 a.m., watching tutorials and building plans.

He wasn't lazy.

He wasn't unintelligent.

He wasn't lacking ambition.

HE WAS EXHAUSTING HIMSELF PREPARING FOR A LIFE HE WAS TOO AFRAID TO BEGIN.

And perhaps the most heartbreaking part?

He genuinely believed he was making progress.

💬 BEFORE YOU READ ANY FURTHER, ANSWER THIS HONESTLY:

Have you ever watched someone with fewer qualifications, less knowledge, and fewer resources achieve something you've been planning for years?

You knew more.

You researched more.

You understood the risks better.

You had the better strategy.

Yet somehow...

THEY MOVED FORWARD WHILE YOU REMAINED EXACTLY WHERE YOU STARTED.

If you've experienced this, you're not alone.

And this story might change how you approach the next six months of your life.

❤️ LIKE if you believe taking action matters more than looking perfect.

💬 COMMENT A if you tend to overthink everything, B if you prefer to start and learn, or BOTH if you're somewhere in between.

🔁 SHARE this with someone who has an incredible idea but keeps waiting for the perfect moment.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💔 THE MOST DANGEROUS KIND OF PROCRASTINATION IS THE KIND THAT MAKES YOU FEEL PRODUCTIVE.

Sometimes procrastination doesn't look like lying on the sofa.

Sometimes it looks like working incredibly hard.

It looks like waking up early.

Buying another course.

Reading another book.

Watching another tutorial.

Redesigning your website for the seventh time.

Comparing software you haven't even needed yet.

Creating a five-year business strategy before speaking to your first customer.

And every evening, you go to bed exhausted.

You tell yourself:

"At least I'm working toward something."

But deep down, there's a question you don't want to answer.

"WHAT DID I ACTUALLY DO TODAY THAT BROUGHT ME CLOSER TO THE RESULT I WANT?"

Not what did you learn.

Not what did you organize.

Not what did you plan.

What did you actually test, create, submit, sell, practise, or complete?

Because there's a painful difference between preparing to change your life and actually changing it.

And the longer you confuse the two, the more time can slip away.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

☕ TWO FRIENDS. ONE COFFEE SHOP. ONE DREAM. AND A DECISION THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING.

Let me tell you a fictional story that illustrates something very real.

Daniel and Marcus were both 36.

They'd been friends since university.

Both were married.

Both had children.

Both worked long hours.

Both wanted to build businesses that could eventually give their families more financial security.

Neither was wealthy.

Neither had powerful connections.

Neither had a large amount of money to invest.

But they had ambition.

One Friday evening, Daniel called Marcus.

"Meet me at the coffee shop. I've got something exciting to show you."

When Marcus arrived, Daniel was already sitting at their usual table.

His laptop was open.

A thick notebook sat beside his coffee.

And for the first time in months, Daniel looked genuinely excited.

"Marcus, I've finally figured out how we're going to make money."

Marcus smiled.

"Tell me."

Daniel turned his laptop around.

There were spreadsheets.

Competitor analyses.

Customer profiles.

Branding concepts.

Revenue projections.

Marketing funnels.

Website designs.

A detailed business plan.

Even a comparison of eleven different software platforms.

Marcus was impressed.

"Daniel, this is incredible. How long have you been working on it?"

"Nearly three months."

"Three months?"

"Yes. And I think another three months should be enough to get everything perfect."

Marcus looked at him.

"Have you spoken to any potential customers?"

Daniel hesitated.

"Not yet."

"Why?"

"Because I need to finish the website."

"Okay. But couldn't you talk to customers while you're building it?"

Daniel shook his head.

"I don't want to look unprofessional."

Marcus leaned back.

Then asked something Daniel hadn't considered.

"WHAT IF THE PEOPLE YOU'RE TRYING TO IMPRESS DON'T ACTUALLY CARE ABOUT HALF THE THINGS YOU'RE BUILDING?"

Daniel laughed.

"That's why I need to research everything."

Marcus nodded.

"Maybe. But how will you know what they want if you never ask them?"

Daniel had no answer.

And that night, they made two different decisions.

Daniel decided to continue preparing.

Marcus decided to find ten potential customers.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📱 THE NEXT MORNING, DANIEL OPENED 27 BROWSER TABS. MARCUS OPENED TEN CONVERSATIONS.

Daniel woke up at 5:30 a.m.

He made coffee.

Opened his laptop.

And began working.

He compared website builders.

Studied artificial intelligence tools.

Researched sales funnels.

Watched marketing tutorials.

Read articles about customer acquisition.

By lunchtime, he had learned an enormous amount.

His notebook was full.

His head was spinning.

But he felt proud.

He was becoming an expert.

Meanwhile, Marcus opened a blank document.

He wrote one sentence:

"I help local businesses attract more customer inquiries through simple digital marketing."

No fancy logo.

No expensive website.

No complicated presentation.

He found ten businesses and contacted them.

Seven ignored him.

Two declined.

One replied.

"Can you explain what you offer?"

Marcus stared at the message.

His heart began beating faster.

Suddenly, all his doubts appeared.

What if I say something wrong?

What if he asks a question I can't answer?

What if I look inexperienced?

What if he rejects me?

He almost closed his laptop.

But instead, he typed:

"Absolutely. Could we arrange a short call so I can understand what your business needs?"

The owner agreed.

Marcus had no customer.

No revenue.

No guarantee of success.

But he had something Daniel didn't.

HIS FIRST CONVERSATION WITH SOMEONE WHO MIGHT ACTUALLY PAY HIM.

That evening, Daniel called.

"What did you do today?"

Marcus replied, "I spoke to a business owner."

"Already?"

"Yes."

"What did he say?"

"He told me he doesn't need most of the services I was planning to offer."

Daniel laughed.

"See! That's why you should have researched more."

Marcus paused.

Then replied:

"DANIEL, THAT WAS THE RESEARCH."

And that one sentence revealed the difference between them.

Daniel was researching what customers might want.

Marcus was discovering what customers actually wanted.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⏳ THIRTY DAYS LATER, ONE MAN HAD A BEAUTIFUL WEBSITE. THE OTHER HAD HIS FIRST PAYING CUSTOMER.

When the friends met again, Daniel looked tired.

He'd redesigned his logo four times.

Purchased three software subscriptions.

Completed another online course.

And almost finished his website.

Marcus asked how things were going.

"Great," Daniel replied. "I'm nearly ready."

"Have you spoken to any customers?"

"Not yet."

Marcus nodded.

Daniel asked, "What about you?"

Marcus looked down.

"Honestly? It's been difficult."

Daniel leaned forward.

"Why?"

"People have ignored me. Some said my service was too expensive. One person told me my proposal wasn't very good."

Daniel shook his head.

"That's exactly what I was worried about."

Marcus continued.

"But one business owner gave me a chance."

Daniel froze.

"What do you mean?"

"He paid me to complete a small project."

Daniel stared.

"Someone actually paid you?"

"Yes."

"Without a website?"

"Yes."

"Without professional branding?"

"Yes."

"Without all the software?"

Marcus smiled.

"Yes."

Daniel went quiet.

Then asked:

"How?"

Marcus answered:

"I STOPPED TRYING TO LOOK LIKE I HAD A SUCCESSFUL BUSINESS AND STARTED TRYING TO HELP SOMEONE WITH A REAL PROBLEM."

For the first time, Daniel felt uncomfortable about all the work he'd done.

Not because the work was worthless.

But because he was beginning to realize something.

His preparation had slowly become a hiding place.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧠💔 SOMETIMES PERFECTIONISM ISN'T ABOUT WANTING EXCELLENCE. IT'S ABOUT BEING TERRIFIED OF NOT BEING GOOD ENOUGH.

Think about that.

As long as your dream remains a plan, nobody can reject it.

As long as your book remains unfinished, nobody can criticize it.

As long as your business remains unlaunched, nobody can tell you they don't want your service.

As long as your YouTube channel remains an idea, nobody can ignore your videos.

As long as your job application remains a draft, nobody can say no.

Your dream remains safe.

Untouched.

Unchallenged.

Perfect.

But there's a terrible price for that protection.

THE SAME WALL THAT PROTECTS YOUR DREAM FROM FAILURE CAN ALSO PREVENT IT FROM EVER BECOMING REAL.

Perhaps you've spent years being the person who always gets things right.

Perhaps people have praised your intelligence.

Perhaps you're afraid of disappointing your family.

Perhaps you've failed before, and you don't want to experience that pain again.

So you prepare.

And prepare.

And prepare.

Until preparation becomes easier than facing the possibility of rejection.

But here's what I want you to understand.

❤️ BEING A BEGINNER IS NOT SOMETHING TO BE ASHAMED OF.

Every successful entrepreneur once had no customers.

Every confident speaker once struggled to find the right words.

Every experienced teacher once taught a first lesson.

Every successful creator once published something that wasn't perfect.

Every skilled professional once had questions they were embarrassed to ask.

The difference isn't that successful people never feel afraid.

It's that many of them learn how to act responsibly while uncertainty still exists.

Your first attempt doesn't have to be impressive.

It has to give you somewhere to begin.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🚪 IMAGINE SPENDING SIX MONTHS LEARNING HOW TO OPEN A DOOR THAT WAS NEVER LOCKED.

Two people stand in front of a closed door.

The first examines it carefully.

Studies the hinges.

Researches the manufacturer.

Watches tutorials about locking systems.

Compares locksmiths.

Creates a detailed plan.

Then says:

"I think I'll be ready to open it next month."

The second person walks forward.

Places a hand on the handle.

Turns it.

And the door opens.

The first person stares in disbelief.

"How did you know it wasn't locked?"

The second replies:

"I DIDN'T. THAT'S WHY I TRIED THE HANDLE."

Sometimes life is like that.

We spend months solving problems that may not even exist.

We imagine rejection before anyone has rejected us.

We prepare for criticism before anyone has seen our work.

We spend money on tools before discovering whether we need them.

We build complicated systems before completing one simple task.

And sometimes, the greatest breakthrough isn't discovering a better strategy.

It's discovering that the first step was much smaller than we imagined.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌙 SIX MONTHS LATER, THE TWO FRIENDS RETURNED TO THE SAME COFFEE SHOP.

Daniel arrived first.

His laptop was open.

His website was finally finished.

It looked beautiful.

The branding was excellent.

The pages loaded quickly.

The presentation was professional.

Everything was exactly as he'd imagined.

But his business had a problem.

He still had no paying customers.

Marcus arrived twenty minutes later.

He looked exhausted.

But there was something different about him.

He seemed calmer.

More confident.

More comfortable discussing business.

Daniel noticed immediately.

"How are things going?"

Marcus smiled.

"Not perfectly."

He explained that he'd lost a customer.

Underpriced a project.

Made mistakes.

Received criticism.

Spent sleepless nights wondering whether he'd made the right decision.

There were moments when he'd wanted to quit.

But he'd also completed several paid projects.

Improved his services.

Built relationships.

Learned how to communicate with customers.

And discovered what businesses were actually willing to pay for.

He wasn't rich.

He hadn't achieved financial freedom.

He wasn't driving a luxury car.

But he had something that couldn't be purchased through another online course.

SIX MONTHS OF REAL EXPERIENCE.

Daniel listened quietly.

Then asked the question that had been bothering him.

"Marcus, can I ask you something?"

"Of course."

"How did you get so far when you knew so much less than me?"

Marcus looked at his friend.

He knew how hard Daniel had worked.

He knew how many evenings he'd sacrificed.

He knew how badly he wanted to succeed.

So he answered carefully.

"Daniel, you wanted to know everything before you began."

"I wanted to learn what mattered by beginning."

"You were trying to avoid every mistake."

"I was trying to make mistakes small enough to recover from."

"You wanted to know what customers would say."

"I asked them."

"You wanted the perfect offer."

"I tested an imperfect one and improved it."

Then Marcus said something Daniel would never forget.

"I WAS WILLING TO LOOK LIKE A BEGINNER WHILE YOU WERE STILL TRYING TO LOOK LIKE AN EXPERT."

Daniel lowered his eyes.

For a moment, he said nothing.

Then whispered:

"I think I've wasted six months of my life."

Marcus shook his head.

"No, Daniel. You've learned a lot. Your knowledge might become a real advantage."

"But there's something you need to understand."

Daniel looked up.

"What's that?"

"YOU CAN'T LEARN TO SWIM BY SPENDING YOUR ENTIRE LIFE READING ABOUT WATER."

Daniel smiled faintly.

Then his expression changed.

He thought about his children.

The evenings he'd missed.

The weekends he'd spent behind his laptop.

The promises he'd made to himself.

He remembered telling his wife:

"Just a few more weeks, and I'll finally be ready."

And suddenly, he realized he'd been saying the same thing for half a year.

His voice trembled.

"What if I try and fail?"

Marcus leaned forward.

"Then you'll learn something you didn't know yesterday."

"What if nobody wants my service?"

"Then you'll have a real reason to improve it."

"What if people think I'm inexperienced?"

"Then be honest about what you can do and demonstrate your value."

Daniel stared at his coffee.

Then asked quietly:

"What would you do if you were me?"

Marcus smiled.

"TOMORROW, CONTACT TEN POTENTIAL CUSTOMERS."

Daniel laughed nervously.

"That's it?"

"That's your first step."

"What if all ten reject me?"

Marcus replied:

"THEN YOU'LL HAVE TEN REAL RESPONSES TO LEARN FROM INSTEAD OF ANOTHER HUNDRED IMAGINARY PROBLEMS TO WORRY ABOUT."

Daniel closed his laptop.

For the first time in six months, he wasn't thinking about redesigning his website.

He wasn't thinking about buying another course.

He wasn't thinking about finding the perfect software.

He was thinking about speaking to his first customer.

And something changed.

He still felt afraid.

He still didn't have all the answers.

But for the first time, he was willing to begin without them.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

❤️ THE NEXT MORNING, DANIEL DID SOMETHING THAT SIX MONTHS OF PREPARATION HADN'T GIVEN HIM THE COURAGE TO DO.

He opened his laptop.

But this time, he didn't open another tutorial.

He didn't check his website.

He didn't compare software.

He wrote a message to a local business owner.

He read it.

Changed a sentence.

Read it again.

His finger hovered over the send button.

For a moment, the familiar thoughts returned.

"What if this sounds unprofessional?"

"What if he ignores me?"

"What if I'm not ready?"

Then he remembered Marcus's words.

"YOU DON'T NEED TO LOOK LIKE AN EXPERT TO TAKE YOUR FIRST STEP."

He pressed send.

Nothing dramatic happened.

No money appeared.

No customer immediately replied.

No magical opportunity arrived.

But Daniel sat back in his chair.

And smiled.

Because after 180 days of preparing to start...

HE HAD FINALLY STARTED.

That evening, his young daughter walked into his office.

"Daddy, are you working again?"

Daniel looked at her.

Then at his laptop.

He closed it.

"Not tonight, sweetheart."

She smiled.

"Can we play?"

He took her hand.

"Of course."

And as they walked into the living room, Daniel realized something else.

He didn't need to sacrifice every evening to prove he was serious about his future.

He needed to spend his working hours on actions that mattered.

And make room for the life he was trying to improve.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔥 HERE ARE FIVE THINGS I HOPE YOU REMEMBER LONG AFTER YOU FINISH READING THIS.

1. BEING BUSY IS NOT THE SAME AS MOVING FORWARD.

You can work twelve hours a day and still avoid the most important task.

Ask yourself whether today's work created something useful, tested an assumption, or moved a meaningful goal forward.

2. YOUR FIRST VERSION DOESN'T HAVE TO BE YOUR BEST VERSION.

Your first video may receive twenty views.

Your first offer may be rejected.

Your first presentation may feel awkward.

Your first project may reveal weaknesses.

That doesn't mean you should stop.

It means you've gained information you can use to improve.

3. REJECTION IS UNCOMFORTABLE, BUT ENDLESS UNCERTAINTY CAN BE EXHAUSTING.

A rejected proposal can teach you what needs changing.

An unanswered message can encourage you to try a different approach.

Feedback can reveal problems you couldn't see alone.

Not every rejection contains a useful lesson, but real responses often provide more direction than endless guessing.

4. SIMPLICITY IS NOT THE SAME AS CARELESSNESS.

Don't rush decisions that involve serious financial, medical, legal, engineering, or safety consequences.

Prepare thoroughly when mistakes could cause significant harm.

But when a step is small, responsible, affordable, and reversible, don't automatically turn it into a six-month project.

5. YOU DO NOT HAVE TO FEEL READY TO BEGIN LEARNING.

Confidence often grows through experience.

You can prepare sensibly, take one manageable step, evaluate the result, and improve.

You don't have to know the entire journey before taking the next step.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💔 NOW I WANT TO ASK YOU A QUESTION THAT MIGHT BE UNCOMFORTABLE.

What have you been postponing?

That business idea?

That YouTube channel?

That book?

That job application?

That new skill?

That conversation?

That opportunity you've been talking about for years?

How many times have you said:

"I'll start next Monday."

"I'll do it when I have more money."

"I'll begin when I understand everything."

"I'll launch when my website is perfect."

"I'll apply when my résumé is better."

"I'll create content when I have the right equipment."

And how many months have passed since you first said those words?

Here's something worth remembering.

SIX MONTHS FROM NOW, YOU WILL HAVE SPENT THOSE SIX MONTHS REGARDLESS OF WHETHER YOU STARTED.

You could spend them researching the same questions.

Or you could spend them testing small ideas, developing skills, gathering feedback, and learning what actually works.

Neither path guarantees success.

But only one gives your idea a chance to encounter the real world.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

❤️ TO THE PERSON WHO HAS BEEN WAITING FOR THE PERFECT MOMENT...

You are allowed to be inexperienced.

You are allowed to ask questions.

You are allowed to create something that needs improvement.

You are allowed to change direction after learning something new.

You are allowed to be nervous.

You are allowed to begin small.

You do not have to become careless.

You do not have to abandon your standards.

You do not have to pretend you know things you haven't learned.

And you certainly don't have to risk everything to prove you're serious.

But please don't spend your entire life believing that your dreams must remain untouched until you can guarantee success.

Because there may never be a day when every doubt disappears.

There may never be a morning when you wake up knowing every answer.

And there may never be a perfect moment when the world promises that nothing will go wrong.

YOU DON'T NEED A GUARANTEE THAT EVERYTHING WILL WORK. YOU NEED A RESPONSIBLE FIRST STEP THAT GIVES YOU SOMETHING REAL TO LEARN FROM.

One conversation.

One application.

One useful video.

One small project.

One honest attempt.

And then another.

And another.

Until the person you once imagined becoming begins to take shape through the things you actually do.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💬 BEFORE YOU GO, I WANT TO HEAR FROM YOU.

If you could go back six months and give yourself one piece of advice, what would it be?

Would you say:

🅰️ "STOP OVERTHINKING AND START."

🅱️ "PREPARE, BUT DON'T HIDE BEHIND PREPARATION."

❤️ Or would you tell yourself something completely different?

COMMENT A, B, OR SHARE YOUR OWN ADVICE.

Your answer might be exactly what someone else needs to read today.

❤️ LIKE if this story made you think about something you've been postponing.

🔁 REPOST it for the person who's been working so hard to get ready that they've forgotten to begin.

And remember this:

THE PERSON WHO STARTS IMPERFECTLY TODAY MAY BE SIX MONTHS AHEAD OF THE PERSON WHO WAITS SIX MONTHS TO START PERFECTLY.

DON'T LET THE FEAR OF LOOKING LIKE A BEGINNER PREVENT YOU FROM EVER BECOMING EXPERIENCED. ❤️

Nothing is rushing.

The view opens up around you, light sliding across whatever is in front of you, and for a few quiet minutes the day belongs only to you and the steam rising off the cup.

Coffee outside doesn’t just wake you up; it resets the pace.

The breeze moves, the light shifts, and the world feels a little wider than it did indoors.

One cup, one stretch of morning air, and the rest of the day starts from somewhere better than a kitchen counter.

Go get it.

The breeze is already waiting.

GM gSleep,

The next big opportunity in digital wellness may not be collecting more health data.

It may be building a system that understands the person behind the data.

Two people can get the same amount of sleep and wake up feeling completely different. Their routines, habits, nutrition, activity and individual patterns all influence how they feel.

A sleep score alone cannot capture that entire picture.

This is why @sleepagotchi's broader direction is worth watching.

Sleep creates a natural starting point because it gives the system a recurring signal every morning. But the real opportunity is connecting that signal with other parts of everyday life.

The Sleep Coach can interpret what happened overnight.

The Wellness Coach can extend that context into daily habits and activity.

The Meal Planner can help connect personal needs with nutrition decisions.

And the Shopping Agent could eventually help users act on relevant recommendations.

Each agent addresses a different part of the journey, but the bigger value comes from connecting them.

Instead of receiving isolated advice from separate apps, users could move toward a more coordinated wellness experience that becomes increasingly relevant to their routines.

That is the difference between personalization as a feature and personalization as the foundation of a product.

Of course, this vision depends on execution. The recommendations must be genuinely useful, the agents must work together reliably, and users must remain in control of their sensitive health information.

But if those pieces come together, Sleepagotchi could offer something more meaningful than another place to check a sleep score.

A system that doesn't just measure your habits, but helps you understand them and make better decisions over time.

Sleep is the starting signal.

Understanding the individual is the bigger ambition.

And earning the user's trust every day is what could make the entire model work.

text:
History has a strange way of being rewritten to suit a modern blame game. 

Today, the cultural narrative fiercely assigns the entire weight of abortion and feminism to women—either framing it as their exclusive victory or blaming them as the sole architects of a crumbling social structure. But history rejects this lopsided finger-pointing. When you strip away the contemporary political theater and look at the facts, you find a shared human reality: historically, men and women almost equally wanted access to abortion, driven by overlapping needs for population control, economic survival, and a shared desire to avoid the life-altering responsibilities of unplanned parenthood.

Long before it became a battleground of identity politics, reproductive regulation was a pragmatic tool. In ancient Greece and Rome, male philosophers and leaders openly advocated for abortion to prevent overcrowding and protect state resources. For centuries, under English common law, early legal structures implicitly allowed the practice prior to "quickening." Men and women alike leaned on these boundaries—women to protect their health and secure a future, and men to escape the financial and social liabilities of sudden fatherhood in societies that offered no safety nets.

It wasn't until the late 1800s that a sudden shift occurred. An all-male medical establishment, seeking a professional monopoly over female midwives and driven by demographic anxieties, actively campaigned to criminalize abortion across America. In doing so, they took a practice that both sexes had relied on for survival and drove it into the shadows.
When the pendulum finally swung back toward legalization in the 20th century, it wasn't a rogue faction of women who built the new system. It was, once again, engineered by men.

They convince you that women are the root of the problem, but the entire foundation of the feminist movement was actually started and funded by men.
The very term "feminism" was coined in 1837 by French philosopher Charles Fourier. In America, early women's rights initiatives were heavily financed and sustained by wealthy male donors, because women historically lacked legal control over property and wealth. Abolitionist Francis Jackson and businessman Charles Hovey provided the massive financial trusts that kept the suffrage movement afloat, while prominent male leaders like Frederick Douglass were foundational in organizing and pushing for women's rights at early conventions like Seneca Falls. Men built the structural and financial runway for feminism long before it became a mainstream cultural shift.

The exact same thing happened with abortion. While feminists get blamed for it today, the modern abortion movement was entirely engineered by men.
The modern political movement to legalize it was launched by male activists, while the founder of birth control, Margaret Sanger, strongly opposed abortion as a danger to public health. 

Before the Supreme Court ever stepped in, male governors and lawmakers completely engineered state legalization bills:

* Colorado (1967): Introduced by Rep. Richard Lamm, signed by Gov. John Love.
* California (1967): Sponsored by Sen. Anthony Beilenson, signed by Gov. Ronald Reagan.
* New York (1970): Sponsored by Sen. Franz Leichter, pushed and signed by Gov. Nelson Rockefeller, with the tie broken by Assemblyman George Michaels.
* Hawaii (1970): Passed by a heavily male legislature and signed by Gov. John A. Burns.
* Alaska (1970): Passed by male legislators overriding a veto by Gov. Keith Miller.
* Washington (1970): Pushed by a male-dominated legislature to a referendum vote.

Finally, in 1973, an all-male, entirely Christian Supreme Court bench voted 7-2 to legalize it nationwide, with Justice Harry Blackmun authoring the landmark decision. From the coining of feminism to the signing of abortion laws, men built the entire infrastructure.

True accountability demands that we look at this history clearly. When men attack women today over these issues, it reveals a profound irony and a deep-seated accountability problem. You cannot historical-engineer a system, utilize it for centuries to manage your own financial and personal liabilities, construct the legal frameworks to codify it, and then turn around and blame women for its existence. History is a two-way street, and the infrastructure of our modern world was built by both hands.

Congressman Sherman, first of all, thank you for speaking out against the executions in Iran and supporting the Iranian people.

The Islamic Republic is now taking revenge on the Iranian people for the January uprising.
I believe economic sanctions, airstrikes, and even limited ground operations will never be enough on their own to bring down this regime.
To develop an effective strategy against the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism, we must first listen to the real voice of the Iranian people.
