Long Turkish War (1593-1606)  Particularly associated with:  Siege warfare Devastated villages Plague outbreaks  Exactly the sort of historical background that later produced dark folklore.  Spain Reconquista  A centuries-long struggle between Christian and Muslim kingdoms.  Gothic remains:  Desert monasteries Border castles Mountain fortresses  Many Spanish ghost stories occur in former frontier zones.  Peninsular War (1808-1814)  Napoleonic invasion.  Famous for:  Ruined abbeys Devastated villages Guerrilla warfare  Many Spanish haunting legends emerged after this period.  Africa Ethiopian-Adal Wars  One of the most dramatic religious wars in African history.  Gothic imagery:  Rock-hewn churches Burned monasteries Mountain sanctuaries  The Ethiopian Highlands have an atmosphere surprisingly similar to some Armenian mountain regions.  Mahdist War (Sudan)  Known for:  Desert battlefields Isolated forts Religious visions and prophecies  Creates a very different but equally haunting landscape.  Which Region Feels Most Like Gothic Armenia?  For someone interested in Ani, khachkars, ruined monasteries, winter folklore, and cross legends, the closest comparisons are:  Eastern Anatolia and Armenia (Ani, Kars, Van) Georgia (Tao-Klarjeti ruins, mountain monasteries) Medieval Hungary and Transylvania Carpathian Ukraine Ethiopian Highlands  All share:  Frontier warfare Monasteries on cliffs Ancient crosses Sacred mountains Lost settlements Folklore of protection against evil Ruins that inspired legends long after the wars ended  The most haunting Armenian example remains Ani itself: a medieval capital emptied by war, invasions, earthquakes, and shifting trade routes, leaving churches, monasteries, caves, and khachkars standing in silence on the frontier. That combination of real history and later folklore is what gives Ani its uniquely gothic character.  Provide your feedback on BizChat If we focus specifically on Ani and its immediate frontier region, the city's history is essentially a succession of wars, sieges, invasions, and shifting empires. This is one reason Ani feels so "gothic" today. The ruins are not the remains of a city destroyed in one event. They are the result of centuries of conflict.  1. The Bagratid-Arab Frontier  Before Ani became Armenia's capital, it stood in a borderland contested between Armenian rulers and Arab emirates.  Historical reality The Bagratid Armenian kings gradually expanded their power. Frontier fortresses guarded river crossings and trade routes. Noble houses competed for influence. Gothic atmosphere  Imagine:  Beacon fires on distant hills Armed horsemen crossing snowy plains Monasteries acting as frontier refuges Khachkars standing beside military roads  This is the world from which Ani emerged.  2. Byzantine Takeover of Ani (1045)  One of the most important events in Ani's history.  Historical fact  The Byzantine Empire absorbed the Armenian kingdom, and Ani passed under Byzantine control.  Gothic consequence  Many Armenians later viewed this as the end of an independent golden age.  In folklore and national memory this event can feel almost like:  A kingless city awaiting disaster.  Because only decades later a much greater threat arrived.  3. The Seljuk Capture of Ani (1064)  This is perhaps the most famous war linked to Ani.  Historical fact  The forces of Alp Arslan captured Ani in 1064 after a siege.  Why it matters  Contemporary sources describe extensive destruction during the capture.  For many Armenians this became one of the defining tragedies of medieval Armenian history.  Gothic imagery  This is the source of many later images associated with Ani:  Breached walls Burning churches Fallen banners Empty streets Refugees fleeing into winter  Many of the later legends about cursed ruins and lost grandeur draw emotional power from this event.  4. Georgian-Armenian Reconquest  Ani did not simply vanish after 1064.  Historical fact  Control of the city changed multiple times.  Armenian and Georgian forces later regained influence in the region.  The city experienced periods of recovery and rebuilding.  Gothic element  Ani becomes a city repeatedly rescued and repeatedly endangered.  It survives.  Then falls.  Then revives.  Then falls again.  This cycle gives Ani an almost legendary character.  5. Mongol Invasions (13th Century) Historical fact  The Mongols entered the Caucasus and transformed the political landscape.  Ani came under Mongol domination.  Gothic consequence  The city survived physically but was increasingly weakened.  Trade shifted.  Political centers changed.  The sense of a great city fading began.  Imagine:  Half-empty districts Winds moving through unused buildings Wealth disappearing from former marketplaces 6. Timur's Era  Although Ani was already in decline, the period associated with Timur added to regional instability.  Historical reality  The Caucasus experienced repeated campaigns and devastation.  Folklore  Many local stories later condensed centuries of warfare into tales of a single great catastrophe.  In reality the decline was gradual, but legends often imagine one final night when everything ended.  7. Ottoman-Persian Frontier Wars  For centuries the region containing Ani became a border zone between competing empires.  Historical consequences Military movement through the region Depopulation in some areas Shifting loyalties Economic decline  Many settlements around Ani shrank or disappeared.  Gothic atmosphere  A ruined medieval capital standing in a contested frontier becomes an ideal setting for folklore.  8. Russian-Ottoman Wars  By the nineteenth century the wider Kars region around Ani became strategically important again.  Russian and Ottoman forces repeatedly fought across eastern Anatolia and the Caucasus.  What visitors often forget  When Russian archaeologists first seriously studied Ani, the landscape around the ruins was itself shaped by recent military history.  Ani was not simply a medieval ruin.  It also stood within a modern frontier zone.  Folklore vs History Around Ani History  What actually destroyed Ani?  Not one curse. Not one invasion.  Instead:  Sieges Political changes Shifting trade routes Earthquakes Population decline Frontier warfare  over centuries.  Folklore  People later imagined:  Angels guarding empty churches Bells ringing from ruined monasteries Saints protecting khachkars Lights among the ruins Sacred crosses watching over the abandoned city The Most "Gothic" Moment in Ani's History  If you're seeking the darkest historically grounded scene, it is probably this:  Winter after the Seljuk capture of 1064.  The walls still stand.  The Cathedral still rises above the plateau.  Snow falls through damaged districts.  Merchants are gone.  Refugees have fled.  Monks continue praying in churches surrounded by devastation.  The khachkars remain standing.  And far beyond the walls, wolves cross the frozen steppe.  That image is not legend. It is the kind of landscape that centuries of real warfare around Ani made possible. Ani was not destroyed by a single siege. What makes Ani so fascinating is that it endured waves of sieges, conquests, and recaptures over nearly two centuries.  Why Ani Was So Hard to Capture  Before discussing the sieges, it helps to understand the city's defenses.  Ani sat on a naturally fortified plateau. Deep river gorges protected much of the city, while massive walls defended the more accessible approaches. Medieval writers described it as extraordinarily difficult to conquer.  Imagine:  Cliffs dropping into the Akhurian River. Multiple defensive walls. Narrow approaches. Towers overlooking ravines.  This is one reason so many attackers needed lengthy sieges rather than direct assaults.  First Great Crisis: Byzantine Pressure (1041-1045) Battle of Ani (1042)  After the death of Armenian king Hovhannes-Smbat, the Byzantine Empire attempted to absorb the kingdom.  Armenian forces under Vahram Pahlavouni defeated a Byzantine army attacking Ani. This victory allowed the crowning of Gagik II as king inside Ani's cathedral.  Gothic image  This was one of the last moments of independent royal Ani:  knights riding beneath cathedral towers, banners over the walls, church bells celebrating victory.  But the triumph was temporary.  Fall to Byzantium (1045)  Ani's final loss to Byzantium came more through political maneuvering than through a dramatic storming of the walls.  According to historical accounts, King Gagik II was summoned to Constantinople, and after political pressure and internal divisions, Ani was surrendered to Byzantine control.  History No famous last stand. No burning breach. The kingdom ended through diplomacy and pressure. Why it mattered  The city lost its Armenian royal government just before the Seljuk advance.  The Most Famous Siege: Alp Arslan (1064) Background  By 1064, Ani was under Byzantine control.  Alp Arslan, ruler of the Seljuks, marched into Armenia with an army equipped with siege specialists and siege engines.  Defenders  The city was commanded by Byzantine governors Duke Bagrat and Gregory.  The Siege Begins  The siege lasted about 25 days.  Medieval accounts describe the Seljuks employing sophisticated siege methods:  wooden towers, mangonels and stone-throwers, archers, sapping and undermining operations, artificial earthworks built against the walls.  One account describes a huge wooden tower carrying troops and siege engines close to the walls. Another describes engineered mounds built from earth and straw to raise attackers above defensive positions.  The Breach  Several medieval sources agree that the walls eventually failed.  Accounts differ on the details:  some emphasize mining beneath the walls, others describe parts of the wall collapsing, others mention heavy bombardment by siege engines.  Once the defenses were breached, Seljuk forces entered the city.  The Sack  This became the most traumatic event in Ani's history.  Contemporary and later sources describe:  large-scale killing, mass captivity, looting of the city.  This siege is one of the principal reasons later Armenian memory viewed 1064 as a catastrophe.  The Georgian–Shaddadid Struggle  Many people imagine Ani's history ended in 1064.  It didn't.  Afterward, Ani passed into the hands of the Shaddadids, and over the following century the city became the object of repeated wars involving Georgia and regional Muslim rulers.  Siege of 1124  The Georgian king David IV attacked Ani and captured it from the Shaddadids.  This marks the beginning of a period in which Ani repeatedly changed hands.  Siege of 1161  King George III of Georgia captured Ani. According to historical summaries, a coalition of neighboring Muslim powers then attempted to recover it.  This created a cycle:  capture, reconquest, siege, recovery.  Ani effectively became a frontier city between rival powers.  Siege of 1174  Another major Georgian offensive under George III.  Siege of 1199  Queen Tamar's forces captured Ani again. Under Georgian and Zakarid influence, the city experienced an important revival.  For a time, Ani regained much of its prosperity.  The Mongol Catastrophe Siege and Capture  The Mongols attacked Ani in the 13th century.  Sources agree that the city was captured and devastated in 1236.  The History Museum of Armenia specifically notes that the Mongols captured and destroyed Ani, causing large-scale flight of its population.  Why This Was Different  After earlier conquests, Ani usually recovered.  After the Mongol conquest, recovery became increasingly difficult.  Trade patterns changed, populations moved, and the city's role diminished.  The Final Enemy: Not an Army  The most successful attacker of Ani was not a kingdom.  It was time.  After centuries of warfare:  trade routes shifted, populations declined, earthquakes struck, especially the devastating earthquake of 1319, the city gradually emptied.  By the 17th century, Ani had been abandoned.  History vs. Gothic Memory History  Ani was conquered many times:  Byzantines (1045) Seljuks (1064) Shaddadids Georgians Zakarids Mongols (1236) Gothic Memory  What remains today are:  breached walls, ruined cathedrals, silent monasteries, empty caravan roads, khachkars facing the wind.  The siege most deeply remembered in Armenian historical memory is still the 25-day siege of 1064, when Alp Arslan's army finally broke through what many considered one of the strongest cities in the Caucasus.  Ani was one of the strongest fortified cities in the medieval Caucasus. Its defenses combined natural geography, massive walls, towers, and the weapons of a wealthy royal capital.  Natural Defenses  Ani stood on a plateau almost surrounded by deep river gorges. Medieval writers emphasized that ravines and steep drops protected much of the city, making large-scale assaults difficult except from certain approaches. Attackers could not simply surround the city evenly on all sides.  A defender standing on the walls could look directly down into the ravines below.  The City Walls  Ani's most famous defenses were its enormous walls.  Historical descriptions emphasize:  Multiple defensive lines. Massive stone fortifications. Strong towers. Narrow approaches. Gates protected by defensive works.  The city was considered so formidable that medieval sources described it as extremely difficult to conquer.  A  These weapons helped push enemies back from the walls.  Swords  Used in close fighting.  If enemies entered the city, street fighting would have relied heavily on swords and shields.  Stones and Gravity  One often-forgotten weapon was simply height.  Defenders could drop:  Stones Rubble Heavy objects  onto attackers below.  A city built on cliffs already possessed a major advantage.  Weapons Used Against Ani  The siege of 1064 gives us much clearer information about the attackers' weapons.  The army of Alp Arslan brought specialized siege equipment and engineers.  Mangonels  Large stone-throwing machines were used during the siege.  Simplified:  Plain Text O <- stone   | / \ / \   ====== Frame ======  They hurled rocks at walls and defenders.  Wooden Siege Towers  One source describes a large wooden tower containing soldiers and a mangonel.  Purpose:  Bring archers up to wall height. Shield attackers. Create a platform for assault. Mining and Sapping  Perhaps the most dangerous technique.  Attackers attempted to weaken the walls from below. Sources describe efforts to destroy wall supports and undermine fortifications.  Basic idea:  Plain Text WALL ██████   || ||   Tunnel ========  If enough support was removed, part of the wall could collapse.  Naphtha Weapons  One medieval account mentions naphtha throwers being used during the siege operations.  Naphtha was a flammable substance that could be used in siege warfare.  The Most Impressive Defensive Feature  If I had to choose one thing that made Ani so formidable, it was not a weapon.  It was the combination of:  Deep river gorges. Massive walls. Narrow approaches. Wealth sufficient to maintain strong fortifications.  Medieval observers treated Ani almost like a giant stone fortress-city rather than a typical town. That is why the 25-day siege of 1064 became so famous: many contemporaries regarded the city as nearly impregnable, yet the Seljuk engineers eventually breached its defenses and captured it.  Viewed today from the ruined walls above the Akhurian Gorge, you can still see why generations of Armenians believed Ani could withstand any army. The landscape itself was a weapon. Medieval sieges were usually not dramatic one-day assaults. Most commanders preferred to make a city surrender, because storming fortified walls was expensive, slow, and deadly.    Using Ani as an example, here's how a typical medieval siege worked.    Stage 1: Isolation    The first goal was to surround the city.    Attackers tried to:    Block roads.  Stop supplies entering.  Prevent messengers from leaving.  Cut access to farms and water sources when possible.  Camps  X X X X X    X X

A bone cross is exactly what it sounds like: a cross made from bone, either animal bone or, more rarely in historical contexts, human bone relics. Bone crosses have appeared in various cultures for different reasons:
https://t.co/Sm4YN5iL8a
As religious relic-crosses, containing fragments of saints' bones.
As memento mori symbols, reminding people of mortality.
As protective amulets, believed to ward off evil spirits, misfortune, or disease.
As funerary objects placed with the dead.
https://t.co/OeQDEwn5XU
In Armenian tradition specifically, bone crosses are not among the most famous national symbols, but Armenia has a long history of relic veneration, where fragments of saints' bones were housed in ornate reliquaries, churches, and monastery treasures. A cross that contained relics could be regarded as especially powerful and holy.
https://t.co/975k2ZgaT5
Armenian Cross Folklore and Superstitions
https://t.co/T5gm6fa57A
The cross occupies an unusually important place in Armenian folklore because Armenia was the first kingdom to officially adopt Christianity.
https://t.co/qqrFP5bK9e
1. Crosses as Protection Against Evil

In Armenian folk belief, making the sign of the cross could protect against:

Evil spirits
Demons
The evil eye
Night terrors
Dangerous mountain beings
Unexplained illness

Travelers sometimes crossed themselves before entering isolated valleys, caves, or ruins.

2. Crossroads and Crosses

Throughout Armenian villages, stone crosses and khachkars (cross-stones) were often erected at roads and boundaries.

People believed these crosses:

Marked sacred territory.
Protected communities from harm.
Turned away wandering spirits.
Blessed travelers.

A crossroads without a cross could be considered spiritually vulnerable.

3. Khachkars as Living Guardians

One fascinating Armenian belief held that certain ancient khachkars possessed a kind of spiritual presence.

People sometimes believed:
https://t.co/VWy4Zf7oac
A blessed khachkar protected nearby fields.
Removing one brought bad luck.
Damaging one invited divine punishment.
Praying at a particular khachkar could bring healing.
https://t.co/FNVZujAZZU
These ideas blended Christian devotion with older folk traditions.
https://t.co/D3PEcp3CNP
4. Crosses and Storms
❝A wolf protects their territory like we protect the Norwegian borderline.❞
In some Armenian folk traditions, crosses were invoked during:
https://t.co/1T6277KzHQ
Hailstorms
Lightning storms
Droughts
https://t.co/TlstXAGaSb
Priests might bless fields with a cross or process around villages carrying crosses to ask for protection from destructive weather.
https://t.co/XFgBHKTHyX
5. Crosses and Wolves
https://t.co/QHda3B6mOM
In medieval Armenian mountain folklore, wolves were feared during winter nights.
https://t.co/cicu0UCpkV
Some traditions held that:
https://t.co/Ha7ETZAKVf
Wearing a cross offered protection from both physical wolves and spiritual dangers.
Shepherds carried crosses alongside prayers and charms.
Wolves sometimes appeared symbolically as agents of divine testing or wilderness spirits.
6. The Cross Over Doors
https://t.co/6de2vjsM0P
Many Armenian homes displayed a cross over:
Our Lady, Mediatrix of all Grace ,pray for us
https://t.co/w6WofPWy2A
Entrances
Stables
Barns
He who holds the stars in His hand let Himself be held by a young woman and a carpenter.
https://t.co/XsKBde7A1H
This was believed to:
https://t.co/kGHD4cymsu
Prevent evil from entering.
Protect livestock.
Guard sleeping children.
https://t.co/Q2VJTzEFVr
Such customs survived in some rural areas long after the medieval period.
https://t.co/8l2VJRfWX0
Ani and Cross Legends
https://t.co/Nc28Yz48Pv
Since you've been interested in Ani, there are a few traditions connected to its churches and ruins.
https://t.co/RELQ32PTMM
Local legends say that:
https://t.co/HF7GqMSMOJ
Crosses atop Ani's churches protected the city spiritually.
Angels watched the churches marked by crosses.
Even after the city declined, the sacred power of the cross remained over the abandoned churches.
Prince of the Heavenly Hosts
https://t.co/pWnAAVwAo8
These are legends rather than documented historical facts, but they reflect how deeply the symbol became woven into the cultural memory of Ani.
https://t.co/kBX14xVvep
An Old Armenian Folk Saying
https://t.co/uWryXQjKLz
A traditional type of Armenian blessing might invoke the cross in a protective way:
https://t.co/p4oc1Pkjpn
"May the Holy Cross go before you, behind you, and beside you."
https://t.co/QWTNHN3Eqe
The idea is that the cross acts not merely as a symbol, but as a spiritual guardian accompanying a person through dangerous journeys, dark winters, and uncertain roads.
https://t.co/lbWXzengXS
Given your interest in Ani and gothic lore, the most atmospheric Armenian image is probably an ancient khachkar standing alone in winter snow outside the ruined walls of Ani, believed by villagers to guard the frontier between the living world and the unseen one. Such stories blend Christian faith, medieval memory, and folk superstition in a uniquely Armenian way.
https://t.co/HqwV8E3pfD
Prayer for a miracle/s
https://t.co/vTNv1817oT
Ani Sun Magazine X Protection Against Evil
When it comes to dark Armenian cross legends, it's important to separate folklore from actual church teaching. Armenian Christianity viewed the cross as a symbol of life, victory, and protection, so the darker stories tend to come from folk beliefs surrounding lonely crosses, ruined churches, cemeteries, and wilderness shrines rather than from official religious tradition.
https://t.co/UBoWYPQrEQ
The Weeping Khachkars
“Listen, put it into your heart, my youngest and dearest son, that the thing that frightened you, the thing that afflicted you, is nothing.”
https://t.co/6iRCZugVKy
— Our Lady of Guadalupe
https://t.co/dvxKSVC87F
One of the most persistent types of Armenian legend concerns ancient khachkars (cross-stones) that are said to weep.
St. Michael the Archangel,

defend us in battle.

and do thou,

O Prince of the heavenly hosts,

by the power of God,

and all the evil spirits,

who prowl about the world

seeking the ruin of souls. Amen.

https://t.co/Q1ULUpHGQE
According to village tales:
https://t.co/QCgv1xohFg
A khachkar erected over an unjust death could shed dew-like drops before a disaster.
Some cross-stones were said to darken before war or invasion.

For a city like Ani, this could be difficult because of its natural defenses and rugged terrain.

Stage 2: Reconnaissance
Here are some of the most powerful and traditional Latin prayers focused on longing for heaven, seeking protection against evil, and asking for deliverance from hell.
1. Longing for Heaven & Salvation
*Anima Christi* (Soul of Christ)

*This is a deeply meditative prayer attributed to the 14th century, traditionally prayed after receiving Holy Communion or when seeking spiritual strength and union with God.*

* **Latin:**
> Anima Christi, sanctifica me.
> Corpus Christi, salva me.
> Sanguis Christi, inebria me.
> Aqua lateris Christi, lava me.
> Passio Christi, conforta me.
> O bone Jesu, exaudi me.
> Intra vulnera tua absconde me.
> Ne permittas me separari a te.
> Ab hoste maligno defende me.
> In hora mortis meae voca me,
> Et jube me venire ad te,
> Ut cum Sanctis tuis laudem te
> In saecula saeculorum. Amen.

* **English Translation:**
> Soul of Christ, sanctify me.
> Body of Christ, save me.
> Blood of Christ, inebriate me.
> Water from the side of Christ, wash me.
> Passion of Christ, strengthen me.
> O good Jesus, hear me.
> Within your wounds hide me.
> Permit me not to be separated from you.
> From the wicked enemy, defend me.
> In the hour of my death, call me
> and bid me come to you,
> that with your Saints I may praise you
> forever and ever. Amen.
2. Against Evil & Hell (The Fatima Prayer)
*Oratio Fátima* (The Fatima Decade Prayer)

*Requested by Our Lady of Fatima in 1917, this is commonly recited at the end of each decade of the Rosary as a plea for mercy and protection from eternal damnation.*

* **Latin:**
> Domine Jesu, dimitte nobis debita nostra, libera nos ab igne inferni, duc in caelum omnes animas, praesertim eas, quae misericordiae tuae maxime indigent.

* **English Translation:**
> O my Jesus, forgive us our sins, save us from the fires of hell, lead all souls to heaven, especially those most in need of Thy mercy.

3. Protection Against Evil (The St. Michael Prayer)
 *Sancte Michael Archangele* (Prayer to St. Michael)

*Pope Leo XIII composed this powerful exorcism prayer for protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil.*

* **Latin:**
> Sancte Michael Archangele, defende nos in praelio, contra nequidias et insidias diaboli esto praesidium. Imperet illi Deus, supplices deprecamur: tuque, Princeps militiae caelestis, Satanam aliosque spiritus malignos, qui ad perditionem animarum pervagantur in mundo, divina virtute, in infernum detrude. Amen.

* **English Translation:**
> Saint Michael the Archangel, defend us in battle. Be our protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil; May God rebuke him, we humbly pray; And do thou, O Prince of the Heavenly Host, by the power of God, thrust into hell Satan and all the evil spirits who wander through the world seeking the ruin of souls. Amen.

 4. General Protection from Evil
 *Sub Tuum Praesidium* (Beneath Thy Protection)

*One of the oldest known hymns to the Blessed Virgin Mary, asking for her intercession against dangers and evil.*

* **Latin:**
> Sub tuum praesidium confugimus, Sancta Dei Genitoris. Nostras deprecationes ne despicias in necessitatibus, sed a periculis cunctis libera nos semper, Virgo gloriosa et benedicta.

* **English Translation:**
> We fly to thy patronage, O Holy Mother of God; despise not our petitions in our necessities, but deliver us always from all dangers, O glorious and blessed Virgin.

Why Ani Survived So Long

Ani combined nearly every good defensive feature available in the Middle Ages:

text:
108 years ago today, a red-headed farmer from Pall Mall, Tennessee did something in the Argonne Forest that still doesn't seem real.

Alvin York grew up dirt poor, a hard drinker and brawler, until a religious conversion in his twenties changed his whole life. When the draft notice came in 1917, he asked to be exempted as a conscientious objector. His church opposed war and so did he. The Army said no.

His battalion commander spent hours going through the Bible with him, trying to convince him that a man could fight and still be right with God. York went home on leave, prayed on it for two days on a mountainside, and came back ready.

On the morning of October 8, 1918, York was one of 17 men sent to slip behind German lines and knock out machine guns near Chatel-Chehery, France. They surprised a group of Germans and captured them. Then the machine guns on the ridge above opened up. Six Americans were killed instantly and three more went down wounded, including the sergeant in charge.

That left Cpl. York in command of seven men, most of them pinned flat guarding prisoners.

So York went to work. Every time a German gunner raised his head to fire, York shot him. He'd been shooting turkeys in the Tennessee hills since he was a kid and he was not missing at that range. When six Germans charged him with bayonets, he drew his pistol and dropped all six, starting with the last man and working forward, so the ones in front wouldn't realize what was happening.

A German officer, Lt. Paul Vollmer, emptied his pistol at York and missed every shot. Watching his men fall one after another, Vollmer finally called out in English and offered to surrender the whole position if York would stop shooting.

York agreed. Then he used Vollmer to order other German positions to give up as they marched back through the woods.

By the time he reached American lines, York had killed 25 men and was herding 132 prisoners in front of him with a handful of survivors.

When a general told him he'd heard York captured the whole German army, York said "No sir. I got only 132."

He was promoted to sergeant and received the Medal of Honor. New York threw him a ticker tape parade. Companies offered him a fortune to endorse their products and he turned almost all of it down. He went home to Tennessee, married his sweetheart, and spent years raising money to build a school for kids in the mountains who had no shot at an education.

When Hollywood finally made his story in 1941, he agreed partly to fund a Bible school. Gary Cooper won the Oscar for playing him.

The man who didn't want to go to war became the most famous American soldier of it.

text: When will it finally be enough? When will we stop, in effect, playing for Team Trump?  Putin's attacks on the Ukrainian civilian population are growing ever more brutal.  But Trump isn't calling for Putin to finally be put in his place. No: Ukraine needs a new president.  On Saturday, Russian glide bombs struck residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia. 20 dead, including three children. One of them was a six-year-old girl. Her birthday would have been at the end of the month, her grandfather said through tears.  Zelenskyy says this is how Russia thanked him for easing the diesel sanctions: with five glide bombs on residential buildings.  With the man responsible for this war, Trump is closing diesel deals, loosening sanctions, and spreading the lie that Zelenskyy is to blame for everything.  In September, Zelenskyy was still thanking him for the "hellish sanctions" law against Russia. In October, the same Trump loosens sanctions against Russia so the diesel can flow.  Zelenskyy could have ended the war many times by now, Trump piles on. That Ukraine has repeatedly offered ceasefires and Putin rejected them—he lies away in front of running cameras.  When will it be enough for us? When will someone in Europe finally demand economic sanctions against Trump?  But we'll keep wrinkling our noses and otherwise staying silent. At least as long as Europe can't replace the American intelligence data itself.  That's Trump's leverage. Because the biggest concern in Kyiv isn't even his remark about the "new president," but that he might halt intelligence cooperation with Ukraine. According to the Financial Times, the US has already threatened in talks in Miami to restrict cooperation if Ukraine continues its attacks on Russian refineries.  And yet the same Financial Times reported a year ago that US intelligence had spent months helping Kyiv hit exactly those kinds of refineries. When it comes to reconnaissance and especially early warning against missile attacks, there are still sensitive dependencies.  Less reconnaissance means less warning. And less warning can mean more dead. More children under rubble like now in Zaporizhzhia. Trump knows what power this dependency gives him. That's why he can afford such threats.  The rest is almost banal: Already in September, the diesel price in the US had hit a record high of six dollars per gallon, and on November 3rd, the election is held. That diesel is so expensive mainly because of the Iran war, which Trump himself started in February, he conveniently leaves out. The arsonist demands that Ukraine, which is already in flames, now help him put out the fire.  Trump wants Kyiv to spare Putin's refineries so people in Ohio can fill up cheaper. He hasn't made a comparable public demand in this context that Putin finally stop his attacks on Ukrainian cities.  The uncomfortable answer to the question "How much longer?" is therefore: until Europe can close this gap itself. With its own reconnaissance, air defense, and ammunition.  And that's when I wonder how our Europe—with its scientists, engineers, industries, and its enormous economic potential—still hasn't managed, in the fifth year of this war, to have solutions for TODAY.  Not just sometime, when there might not be much left of Ukraine.  And yes, Europe has economic leverage against Washington. The EU has a ready package of countermeasures in the drawer, affecting US imports worth 93 billion euros. At the end of July, the Commission suspended it again, this time without an end date.  In principle, it could be reactivated, though it was created for the trade conflict with the US, not for Trump's Ukraine policy.  But for that, we'd need the guts that the Easter bunny brings us. Europe could hurt the US economically where it hurts. But for that, it would have to be willing to pay a price itself.  And that doesn't sell well at the ballot box or in the balance sheets.  That's why we're faced today with a grotesque situation: Ukraine has been defending itself for more than four and a half years against a Russian war of annihilation.  And the president of its most important ally is doing business with the aggressor, demanding military restraint from the attacked country, and calling for the ouster of its president.  Europe protests. Europe worries. Europe looks to Washington.  Putin keeps bombing. And Trump remains our closest ally. And for lunch today, there are fish sticks.

text:
My perspective hits on a profound, materialist truth about economic power that is experiencing a massive revival in the age of artificial intelligence. Viewing an economy through its energy output strips away financial speculation and reveals its raw physical capacity.

The intersection of my argument with the modern AI and semiconductor landscape highlights how energy, chips, and economic supremacy have become completely inseparable.

1. The Materialist View: Watts Equal Wealth

Traditionally, gross domestic product (GDP) can sometimes be inflated by financialization, services and digital abstraction. However, electricity production remains the ultimate ground truth. You cannot fake a megawatt. It reflects heavy industry, manufacturing, transportation, and actual physical productivity. As the old economic maxim goes: energy is the ultimate currency.

2. The AI & Chip Nexus: The New Energy Hunger

The modern artificial intelligence and semiconductor revolution has dramatically supercharged this dynamic:

The Semiconductor Fabs: Advanced chip manufacturing (like extreme ultraviolet lithography used for cutting edge processors) requires immense, uninterrupted power and pristine environmental control.

Data Centers and Training Clusters: Training frontier AI models requires thousands of specialized chips (GPUs) running continuously for months, drawing staggering amounts of electricity. A single major AI data center can consume as much power as a mid-sized city.

The Physical Bottleneck: AI is often discussed as an ethereal, cloud-based phenomenon, but it is fundamentally a heavy industrial enterprise. Code and algorithms are intangible, but the infrastructure hosting them is anchored entirely to the electrical grid.

3. Energy Security as AI Supremacy

Today, the geopolitical race for AI and technological dominance is no longer just about software algorithms or brilliant engineers, it is a race for power generation. Nations and corporations are aggressively locking down clean baseload energy (nuclear, geothermal, and advanced renewables) simply because their future AI compute capacity depends on it.

In the 21st century, electricity production is not just a metric of traditional industrial strength; it has become the primary bottleneck and scorecard for who will lead the next technological era.

Your intuition is spot on: while software creates the intelligence, electricity remains the lifeblood that keeps the machine alive.

- How the geopolitical race for semiconductor manufacturing capacity intersects with national energy grids ?

1. The Raw Scale of Energy Intensity

Modern mega-fabs (such as those run by TSMC, Samsung, and Intel) consume power on a scale equivalent to entire cities:

EUV Lithography: The Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines made by ASML, required to print cutting edge 3nm and 2nm nodes, generate EUV light by vaporizing tin droplets with high power lasers. A single EUV tool consumes up to 1 megawatt of power, roughly 10 times more electricity than previous DUV generations.

Cleanroom Operations: Semiconductor wafers move through hundreds of process steps over several months. This requires industrial scale heating, cooling, ultrafast air filtration, and continuous water purification, demanding an uninterrupted baseline power load.

National Grid Absorption: In Taiwan, TSMC alone accounts for roughly 8% to 10% of the entire island’s electricity consumption. Projections indicate that figure could rise significantly as more advanced nodes scale up.

2. Grid Reliability vs. Micro-Disruptions

For standard manufacturing, a minor power flicker or a 10-second voltage drop is an inconvenience. For a semiconductor foundry, it can be a multimillion-dollar catastrophe:

[ Power Grid Instability / Voltage Sag ]
                 │
                ▼
[ EUV & Chemical Vapor Deposition Tools Halt ]
                 │
                ▼
[ Wafers Ruined + Cleanroom Contaminated ]
                 │
                ▼
[ Months of Re-calibration & Yield Loss ]

Because modern chips feature features measured in nanometers, any variance in power frequency or unexpected shutdown contaminates tool chambers, ruins thousands of silicon wafers in production, and requires weeks to months of tool recalibration.

As a result, governments courting chipmakers cannot simply offer tax breaks; they must guarantee unwavering grid stability backed by dedicated substations, uninterruptible power supply (UPS) infrastructure, and high redundancy.

3. Geopolitical Re-shoring and Grid Constraints

National energy grids are emerging as a major bottleneck in the re-shoring of critical technology supply chains:

United States (Arizona & Ohio): As mega-fabs built by TSMC and Intel expand in the U.S., regional utilities must rapidly expand local transmission lines and generation capacity. These industrial draws compete directly with the surging power requirements of nearby AI data centers.

Taiwan’s Vulnerability: Taiwan’s heavy dependence on imported energy sources leaves its electricity grid geographically concentrated and vulnerable. Energy supply constraints are a key structural reason why chipmakers are diversifying advanced capacity globally.

Europe’s Industrial Cost Challenge: High electricity tariffs and energy grid pressures across Western Europe complicate the economics of building power-hungry foundries, even as the European Union offers heavy capital subsidies.

The geopolitical race for semiconductor capacity is proving that digital independence is impossible without energy capacity. Re-shoring the physical manufacturing of advanced technology requires far more than land and capitaL, it requires national energy grids capable of delivering immense, uninterrupted power. Ultimately, a nation's semiconductor strategy is only as robust as its electrical grid.

text: The Darkest Armenian Monastic Theme  Interestingly, authentic Armenian monastery legends are usually not about monsters.  The darkest theme is abandonment.  A monastery survives invasions, earthquakes, famine, and war.  The monks disappear.  The prayers cease.  The buildings remain.  Then later generations wonder:  Who lit the last candle?  Who rang the last bell?  Who spoke the final prayer before the doors were closed forever?  That melancholy sense of sacred places outliving their communities is one of the most haunting elements in Armenian folklore, especially around Ani, Tatev, Haghpat, Sanahin, and the cave monasteries hidden in the mountains.    Ani Sun Magazine X Protection Against Evil One of the most famous genuine legends connected to Tatev Monastery is the story of the monastery's miraculous pillar, known as the Gavazan ("staff"). The pillar was erected near the monastery in the 10th century and became the center of numerous local legends.  The Legend of the Warning Pillar  According to Armenian tradition, the pillar was not an ordinary monument.  People believed that when danger approached the monastery, the stone column would move or tremble. Monks and villagers saw this as a warning from God that enemies, invaders, or other threats were drawing near. Over time, stories spread that the pillar could sense dangers long before a human lookout could detect them.  In folklore retellings, some monks were said to wake at night feeling the monastery shake. They would look out into the darkness and discover the Gavazan moving slightly against the starlit sky. Soon afterward, hostile forces would reportedly appear on the roads below.  Why the Legend Developed  Historically, Tatev stood in a dramatic and vulnerable location above the deep Vorotan Gorge. The monastery frequently faced threats during periods of invasion and political turmoil.  The pillar itself is real. Because it was engineered in a way that allowed slight movement, unusual vibrations may have helped inspire tales that it could "warn" of approaching danger. Over generations, practical observation transformed into legend.  A Darker Tatev Tradition  A more atmospheric local belief held that the monastery was protected by the prayers of generations of monks who had lived and died there.  On stormy nights, people told stories that the gorge below could fill with mist while the monastery seemed to float above the clouds. Travelers claimed they heard bells, chants, or distant voices carried by the wind from the cliffs. Unlike ghost stories about monsters, these tales reflected a common Armenian theme: a sacred place retaining the memory of centuries of prayer even when no one could be seen. This latter part is folklore associated with monasteries generally rather than a documented miracle of Tatev itself.  Since you're interested in Ani and gothic Armenian lore, Tatev's legend has a similar feeling: not a haunted castle full of specters, but a lonely monastery on the edge of a vast gorge, guarded by a stone pillar that watches the horizon and warns of approaching darkness.    Ani Sun Magazine X Protection Against Evil For Tatev Monastery, it's useful to draw a hard line between what historians know and what later folklore says.  History Tatev Monastery is real  was founded in the 9th century and became one of medieval Armenia's most important religious, educational, and cultural centers. It sits dramatically above the Vorotan Gorge.  The Gavazan pillar is real  The stone pillar called Gavazan ("staff") actually exists at Tatev. It was erected near the monastery and is one of the site's best-known features.  Tatev experienced periods of danger  Like many Armenian monasteries, Tatev existed through centuries of invasions, warfare, and political instability. Monasteries often served as places where manuscripts, learning, and religious traditions were preserved.  Folklore "The pillar warned of approaching enemies"  This is a legend.  Local tradition held that the Gavazan pillar would move or tremble when danger approached the monastery, warning the monks of enemies or impending disaster.  There is no historical evidence that the pillar possessed supernatural powers.  "The monastery was protected by unseen forces"  This is folklore.  Stories developed that divine guardians, saints, or the accumulated prayers of generations of monks protected Tatev from destruction. These stories belong to oral tradition rather than documented history.  "Voices, bells, and chants are heard in the gorge"  This is folklore.  Various local tales describe mysterious sounds around monasteries, especially at night or in fog. I have not found historical sources documenting such events at Tatev specifically. These belong to the broader folklore surrounding remote Armenian monasteries.  What Historians Think About the Pillar  The most interesting part is that the legend may have grown from something real.  The Gavazan was engineered in a way that allowed slight movement. Over time, people may have noticed subtle vibrations and interpreted them as warnings from heaven. The physical object is historical; the supernatural explanation is folklore.  The Darkest Authentic Tradition  The most genuinely haunting aspect of Tatev is not a ghost story at all.  History: monks studied, copied manuscripts, prayed, and lived there for centuries. Folklore: people later imagined that their prayers still lingered in the stones. Reality: when you stand on the cliffs above the gorge today, you are looking at a monastery that survived immense historical upheaval and still stands where countless generations once lived and worshipped.  That blend of real history and later imagination is where most Armenian monastery legends originate. The stone, the monastery, and the people were real; the miracles and warnings belong to folklore.  The Gavazan ("Staff") at Tatev Monastery is one of the most intriguing pieces of medieval Armenian engineering because it was intentionally built to move, even though it appears to be a solid stone monument. It was erected in 906 AD, has an octagonal column, and is topped with a khachkar (cross-stone).  How It Was Built  According to restoration and architectural studies, the structure consists of three main parts:  Khachkar  Movable Stone Pivot  Fixed Foundation  The Key Innovation: A Pivoting Base  The clever part is hidden at the bottom.  The lower pedestal contains:  A fixed foundation stone embedded in the ground. An upper stone connected through a movable hinge-like joint.  Because of this joint, the entire pillar could sway when shaken by:  Earthquakes. Ground tremors. Possibly vibrations traveling through the earth.  After moving, the column would gradually return to its upright position.  History vs. Folklore  History  The movable base is real. The column can swing when disturbed. It was built in 906 AD and still survives.  Folklore  The pillar warned monks of approaching enemy armies. The mysterious movement was believed by some to have supernatural significance. Was It Really a Medieval Seismograph?  Some modern writers describe Gavazan as an early seismograph because it reacted to earth tremors.  However, historians cannot fully prove the builders' exact intention. The monument was unquestionably designed to move, but whether its primary purpose was detecting earthquakes, warning of approaching armies, symbolic theology, or a combination of these remains debated.  Why It's So Remarkable  What makes Gavazan extraordinary is that medieval Armenian builders created a tall stone monument with a controlled moving joint over 1,100 years ago, and it survived centuries of earthquakes and invasions. Restoration specialists describe it as the only known medieval Armenian column intentionally designed to swing and then return to vertical position.  For someone standing in Tatev's courtyard a thousand years ago, seeing an eight-meter stone cross-column suddenly begin to sway while the earth seemed still would have been unsettling enough to inspire legends of divine warnings. Yet beneath the folklore was a genuine feat of Armenian engineering.  Armenian folk beliefs about the cross are especially interesting because they blend ancient pre-Christian ideas about sacred mountains, stones, springs, and boundaries with later Christian symbolism. To a medieval Armenian villager, a cross was often more than a religious emblem. It could be a protective barrier, a witness, a guardian, or a marker between worlds.  1. Protection Against Evil Spirits  This is probably the most widespread folk belief.  People believed the cross could protect against:  Demons Evil spirits Malevolent wandering beings Night terrors Unexplained illness The evil eye  Making the sign of the cross was often the first response to something frightening, especially at night.  In folk belief, evil beings might approach a person, but crossing oneself placed that person under divine protection.  2. Protection Against the Al  One of Armenia's oldest supernatural beings is the Al.  The Al was blamed for:  Childbirth dangers Weakness after birth Night attacks Certain illnesses  Families often placed:  Crosses Prayer books Blessed objects  near mothers and newborn children.  This is one of the clearest examples of Christian symbols being used against older folk demons.  3. Crosses as Boundary Markers  Many khachkars (cross-stones) stood at:  Village entrances Mountain paths Crossroads Bridge approaches Cemetery edges  According to folk belief, such crosses marked a protected space.  The idea was not always that evil could never cross them, but that the cross made the area spiritually defended.  Some villages considered the land within a ring of holy sites and crosses safer than wilderness beyond.  4. Protection for Travelers  Armenia's mountains were dangerous.  Travelers feared:  Bandits Wolves Storms Getting lost  Many people prayed before roadside crosses.  Some believed crossing oneself before entering a mountain pass would bring protection through the journey.  This is particularly common in regions filled with isolated monasteries and highland roads.  5. Wolves and Winter  You have asked before about winter folklore.  In Armenian mountain traditions, wolves often represent the dangerous wilderness beyond human settlement.  Some people carried crosses while herding livestock.  Folk belief sometimes held that:  A blessed cross offered protection. Wolves feared holy places. Churches and monasteries formed safe refuges in winter.  These beliefs varied greatly by region.  6. Khachkars as Guardians  Many Armenians treated ancient khachkars almost as living sacred presences.  Common beliefs included:  Do not damage a khachkar. Do not move one without reason. Do not build with its stones. Do not disrespect it.  Bad luck, crop failure, illness, or misfortune might be blamed on disrespect shown toward a cross-stone.  Even today some villagers treat old khachkars with great reverence.  7. Crosses and Storm Protection  A long-standing tradition involved using the cross during severe weather.  The cross might be carried:  Around fields Through villages During processions  People prayed for protection from:  Hail Lightning Crop destruction Drought  The cross symbolically defended the community against chaos.  8. Oaths Sworn Before a Cross  This belief appears repeatedly in Armenian tales.  A person swearing an oath before a cross was thought to place themselves under divine witness.  Folk belief held:  False oaths would eventually be punished. Betrayal after such a vow brought misfortune. The cross "remembered" the promise.  Many Armenian legends revolve around broken vows and the disasters that follow.  9. Cemetery Crosses  Cemetery crosses had special importance.  People often believed:  A maintained grave remained at peace. A fallen cross should be restored. Disturbing graves attracted misfortune.  The cross served as both a memorial and a spiritual safeguard.  10. Monasteries as Protective Islands  A fascinating Armenian belief is that monasteries created a zone of protection around themselves.  This appears in many local stories.  The monastery was viewed as:  A refuge from war A refuge from storms A refuge from demonic forces A place where constant prayer strengthened sacred power  This may help explain legends surrounding places like Ani, Tatev, Geghard, Haghpat, and Sanahin.  11. The Gavazan of Tatev  This is where folklore and engineering meet.  Historical fact  The Gavazan at Tatev Monastery was a real movable stone column with an articulated pivot joint. It could sway when disturbed and return to vertical position.  Folk belief  People came to believe:  It warned of approaching enemies. It sensed danger. It protected the monastery. Divine power moved it.  The actual movement of the pillar likely helped create these legendary interpretations.  12. The Deepest Armenian Idea  Perhaps the oldest surviving theme is this:  The cross stands where order meets chaos.  In Armenian folklore, crosses often appear at:  Cliffs Roads Mountain passes Monastery gates Graveyards Frontier regions  These are all places that feel like thresholds.  Because of this, crosses became symbols not only of Christianity but of protection at the edge of the known world.  For someone living near the ruins of Ani a thousand years ago, a lone khachkar standing in snow outside the city walls was not merely a monument. In folk imagination it was a silent guardian watching the boundary between the village, the wilderness, the living, the dead, and the unseen. Armenian and Georgian traditions share a great deal because both peoples lived in the Caucasus, adopted Christianity early, built mountain monasteries, and preserved older folk beliefs beneath a Christian layer. Yet they developed distinct spiritual atmospheres.  Similarities 1. Crosses as Protection  In both Armenia and Georgia, crosses were believed to protect against:  Evil spirits Misfortune Disease Dangerous places Unseen forces  Crosses were placed on:  Churches Mountain passes Village entrances Graves  A traveler passing an old cross might pray or make the sign of the cross in either tradition.  2. Sacred Mountains  Both cultures viewed mountains as especially holy.  Armenian examples  Ararat Aragats Mountains around Tatev and Geghard  Georgian examples  Kazbek Svaneti highlands Tusheti mountains  The higher the monastery, the more spiritually powerful people often imagined the site to be.  3. Monasteries as Spiritual Fortresses  In both traditions monasteries were not merely churches.  They were seen as:  Places of learning Places of refuge Places of protection Guardians of national identity  This explains why so many legends surround places such as Tatev Monastery and Georgian sites like Gelati or David Gareja.  Major Differences Armenian Tradition: Stone Guardians  Armenian folklore places an extraordinary emphasis on khachkars.  A khachkar is not simply decoration.  Many folk traditions treated ancient cross-stones as:  Protectors Memorial guardians Sacred boundary markers Witnesses to oaths  You often find an Armenian spiritual landscape marked by solitary crosses standing in fields, mountain passes, cemeteries, and ruins.  The atmosphere is often:  Ancient stone watching silently.  This fits places like Ani, where ruined churches and khachkars became symbols of memory and loss.  Georgian Tradition: Saints and Sacred Places  Georgian folklore tends to focus more heavily on:  Warrior saints Miracle-working icons Sacred springs Guardian churches  Many Georgian stories involve direct intervention by saints, particularly:  Saint George Saint Nino  Saint George is especially important in Georgian folk belief and often appears almost like a legendary protector of the land.  Evil Spirits Armenian  Armenian folklore preserved several old beings including:  Al Devs Kajs Various mountain spirits  Many of these have roots extending back before Christianity.  The cross became a weapon against these older supernatural beings.  Georgian  Georgian folklore also preserved pre-Christian supernatural beings such as:  Ocho-Kochi Devi Forest spirits Water spirits  But Georgian stories often place greater emphasis on saints defeating or overcoming such beings.  Haunted Places Armenian Haunted Places  Armenian legends often attach themselves to:  Ruins Lost cities Abandoned monasteries Deserted churches  The haunting feeling comes from absence.  A common Armenian question is:  Who used to live here?  This is one reason Ani feels so legendary.  Georgian Haunted Places  Georgian stories are often more dramatic.  You find tales of:  Hidden treasures Dragon slayers Hermit saints Miracle-working icons Sacred caves  The focus is often on supernatural encounters rather than abandoned memory.  Tatev vs Georgian Mountain Monasteries  Take the Gavazan at Tatev.  Armenian Interpretation  The pillar itself became legendary.  People focused on the stone structure.  Questions became:  Why does it move? How does it warn of danger? Is it protecting us?  The object acquires folklore.  Georgian Interpretation  A similar story in Georgia would often focus more on:  A saint causing the miracle A relic causing the miracle Divine intervention through a holy figure  The person is usually at the center rather than the monument.  The Deep Cultural Difference  If I had to summarize the feeling of the two traditions:  Armenian Folk Spirituality Ancient Stone-centered Memory-centered Protective crosses Ruins and lost kingdoms Sacred mountains Endurance through suffering  Symbolically:  A khachkar standing alone in the snow beside the ruins of Ani.  Georgian Folk Spirituality Heroic Saint-centered Miracle-centered Sacred churches Living pilgrimage traditions Mountain warriors and hermits  Symbolically:  A mountain church beneath Kazbek protected by Saint George.  Both traditions are deeply Christian, but Armenian folklore often feels more haunted by history and memory, while Georgian folklore often feels more animated by saints, miracles, and living mountain traditions. For someone interested in gothic themes, Armenian legends tend to evoke ruined monasteries, lonely khachkars, winter winds, and the lingering presence of lost kingdoms, whereas Georgian legends more often evoke warrior saints, miraculous icons, and dramatic encounters in the mountains.   I'll focus on the wars that left behind the kinds of landscapes associated with Ani, Tatev, ruined churches, haunted folklore, and frontier legends.  Armenia and Eastern Anatolia (modern Turkey) Arab-Armenian Wars (7th-9th centuries)  These campaigns transformed many Armenian mountain fortresses and monasteries into frontier strongholds.  Gothic elements:  Burned monasteries Deserted mountain settlements Isolated monks living on the frontier Churches surrounded by wilderness  Many Armenian folk stories about hidden treasures and forgotten monasteries originated in regions repeatedly attacked during this era.  Byzantine-Armenian Conflicts  As Armenian kingdoms were absorbed by the Byzantine Empire, noble houses vanished and old fortresses were abandoned.  Gothic imagery:  Empty palaces Fallen noble families Lost royal tombs Seljuk Invasions (11th century)  One of the great turning points in Armenian history.  The Seljuk Turks entered Armenia and Anatolia, leading to destruction and population movements.  Gothic consequences:  Ruined cities Broken churches Empty caravan routes Villages reclaimed by nature  Many visitors today experience Ani's atmosphere partly because centuries of invasions left entire districts abandoned.  Mongol Invasions (13th century)  The Mongol era left deep scars across Armenia and neighboring lands.  Gothic themes:  Burned scriptoria Destroyed libraries Monasteries surviving amid devastation Stories of heavenly protection and miracles Ottoman-Persian Wars  For centuries Armenia sat between the Ottoman and Persian empires.  Entire regions changed hands repeatedly.  Landscape effects:  Empty villages Fortified monasteries Refugee routes through mountains  Many Armenian legends involving guardian saints and miraculous escapes date from these troubled centuries.  The Russian Frontier Russo-Turkish Wars  These wars repeatedly crossed the Caucasus.  Gothic atmosphere:  Snow-covered battlefields Isolated forts Mountain passes Frozen campaigns  Eastern Armenia became heavily influenced by Russian military presence during these conflicts.  Caucasian War (1817-1864)  Russia's conquest of the Caucasus created one of history's great mountain-frontier struggles.  Gothic imagery:  Mist-covered peaks Remote watchtowers Forest warfare Mountain strongholds  The setting resembles something out of medieval epic literature.  Ukraine Mongol Invasion of Kyivan Rus'  Many cities were destroyed.  Gothic elements:  Burned cathedrals Deserted settlements Legends of buried church bells Cossack Wars  Ukraine developed a folklore full of haunted steppes, abandoned battlefields, and wandering warriors.  Common themes:  Ghost horsemen Battlefield crosses Lonely chapels Hungary Ottoman-Hungarian Wars  Perhaps one of Europe's most gothic frontier regions.  For centuries Hungary stood on the border between Christian Europe and the Ottoman Empire.  Landscape:  Ruined castles Abandoned monasteries Forgotten watchtowers

text:
OttoGeoGraphica
March, 2003
Sedona, Arizona
(film camera photograph)

When comparing Estes and Sedona in terms of the behavior emanating from their trendsetting, nouveau riche, residents and visitors, Sedona clearly has the trump card: the Sedona vortex experience. There are various locations in the Verde Valley where a person can meditate in a natural power spot, apparently one of the few on earth. The swirling energy felt in such locations can be very spiritual and offer thought-provoking insight into the natural world. Tours are offered for such New Age fare and assistance is given to those seeking such enlightenment, for a fee.

When one travels, one recognizes early on that wherever the most beautiful spots on earth located, small villages spring up, employing people who cater to the visitors. Some residents appear to be more spiritually in tune with the area around them then the hapless visitor; a creature who is ill-dressed, unable to work his camera, and unable to negotiate the towns roadways. The enlightened ones show contempt for the lowly visitor and using subtlety, discourage their return. Boutiques and over-priced specialty shops appear where outgrown downtown stores used to be. Burgers sell for $20.00 and artisans are selling their sculptures for astronomical sums. A Motel 6 is reincarnated as a bed and breakfast. Mini-vans, travel trailers, and motor homes are cursed off the road by some residents whose $100,000 car attempts to upstage the nearby mountains. In fact, with such vanity, one wonders if the mountains and the scenery are really there at all.

The village becomes a place of prestige, a place to spot motion picture stars, trying to get away from their fame and fortune. Pop stars, renting a villa or the best suite or an entire hotel floor, and then proceeding to trash it. Super models and other celebrities along with their sycophants enjoy teasing paparazzi or flaunting on the ski slopes. The affluent preach that the populace should donate time and money to support worthy causes. Time and money are the two assets that they have entirely too much of yet aren’t as willing to freely let go of. Such actions are truly questionable. Villages are name-dropped nightly on entertainment networks and nightly Hollywood based shows: Aspen, Tahoe, Vail, Jackson, Estes Park, Park City, Sundance, Sun Valley, Santa Fe, Telluride, Livingston, Hot Springs, Myrtle Beach, Savannah, and of course Sedona, but I digress.

There is no question that the ‘swirling energy’ of Sedona is felt at a powerful level by those who wish to feel it. An early morning trek up to Devil’s Bridge after a pre-dawn dusting of new snow, just as the morning sun highlights the many rock faces a vibrant orange glow, would awaken and tickle anyone’s soul. Maybe not at the depth of the aforementioned enlightened ones, but even they would surely acknowledge that at Devil’s Bridge this morning, enlightening took place. I don’t know if there is a vortex there, but I do know it was free.

text:
🇮🇳 India's SMR market just crossed a threshold most countries never reach this cleanly.

In July 2026, two announcements landed within days of each other.

Together, they turned India's SMR conversation from "potential" to "imminent."

1️⃣ Five indigenous SMRs by 2033

Atomic Energy Minister Jitendra Singh confirmed the target.

Backed by ~$2.11 billion under the Nuclear Energy Mission in the Union Budget 2025-26.

That's not a pilot. That's a procurement cycle — measured in years, not decades.

2️⃣ Tata Power targets 2032 for India's first privately built nuclear plant

Construction to begin as early as 2028.

Sites shortlisted across at least three states.

The SHANTI Act of 2025 ended six decades of state exclusivity. Within months, Adani incorporated two nuclear subsidiaries. Tata named hard dates.

Private capital is moving faster than most analysts expected.

The three-track programme — and why the distinction matters:

BSMR-200 — 220 MWe pressurised heavy water reactor, BARC
→ Flagship indigenous track, most advanced
→ Detailed Project Report approved
→ Lead unit proposed for Tarapur, Maharashtra
→ Uses components already in serial domestic production — sharply lower first-of-a-kind risk
SMR-55 — 55 MWe
→ For remote locations, defence installations, smaller industrial clusters
→ Serves what the BSMR-200's scale can't
HTGR up to 5 MW — for hydrogen generation
→ Sits outside India's existing technology base
→ The most open avenue for international collaboration of the three
Now the part vendors should read carefully:
India's manufacturing benchmark for the BSMR-200 is ~$3.15 million per MW domestically.

International range: $5.24M to $104.90M per MW.
Larsen & Toubro says India can manufacture SMRs at least 30% cheaper than global competitors.
That cost advantage doesn't lock international suppliers out. It defines the terms they must engage on:

→ Technology content
→ Quality system credentials
→ Localisation willingness
Those matter more here than price leadership alone.
The vendor race is genuinely open:

No binding international agreements signed yet.

NTPC is in active discussions with EDF, Rosatom, Westinghouse, GE Vernova, KHNP, and Holtec — across all three tracks simultaneously.

🇷🇺 Russia holds a structural edge on the pressurised water track through Kudankulam, and has offered deep localisation including technology transfer.

🇺🇸 Holtec's CEO has publicly stated ambitions for up to 200 SMR units in India.

🇮🇳 Adani is in discussions for eight BSMR-200 units in Uttar Pradesh alone.

Indian Railways has also shown interest for its own energy needs.
Why the next five years matter:
The SHANTI Act removed the liability barrier that kept Western vendors out of commercial-scale engagement.

The AERB has confirmed SMR-specific provisions will be incorporated — modular construction, passive safety — creating a technology-neutral framework.

Vendors who engage now with NTPC, BARC, and the new private entrants, with propositions matched to each track, find a differentiated market.

Vendors who wait for the procurement stage find a landscape already shaped by earlier relationships.

The numbers underneath all of this:
→ 100 GW national nuclear target
→ $201 billion cumulative capital required by 2047
→ Global SMR market projected at $300 billion by 2040

India's position is taking structural shape — as deployer today, and eventually as supplier through its cost-competitive manufacturing base.

The window is open.

It won't stay open long.

Yes, it’s a cap, not a floor. Never said it wasn’t. But Illinois has already demonstrated the ability and willingness to spend up to the existing cap. Raising that ceiling matters when you’re a school that’s already spending at the limit.

And where could additional money come from? How about that Larry Gies pledge? Right now we’re already maxing out the cap so there is no room for his money to be used to pay players. But if suddenly there’s a new bucket of player retention funds to fill up, it makes more sense to start funneling his annual $10M pledge toward that rather than stadium projects like the scoreboard that don’t directly impact winning.

Whitman has already shown he’s an incredible fundraiser while also getting the athletic department back in the black. Between major donors, future fundraising, and current athletic revenue, there’s plenty of reason to believe Illinois could fund the additional retention spending.

And we don’t even need to max out the entire $22.5M allowance for it to make a difference. Even another $10M annually dedicated to retaining our own players would be a massive increase in spending flexibility.

And yes, Altmyer left Ole Miss for playing time. That’s literally why my hypothetical included Illinois offering a clear path to starting. The question was whether he’d make that same decision if Ole Miss could offer him significantly more money to stay. Maybe he still leaves, but the financial tradeoff is completely different. That’s what I’ve been saying this entire time.

Which brings us back to Clayton and Barnett, the whole reason this discussion started. They’re already at Illinois. If they develop into major contributors, we’d have considerably more flexibility to compensate them to stay rather than potentially losing them to another program.

March 19, 2020 (and through much of April 2020 in many places). 
In the last 10 years (roughly 2016–2026), the U.S. national average gasoline price never fell below $1 per gallon. The lowest weekly national average was about $1.77/gallon the week of April 27, 2020, during the COVID-19 demand collapse. 
However, individual stations did drop below $1:
•  On March 19, 2020, a BP station in London, Kentucky, became the first reported in the U.S. to sell regular gas at 99 cents per gallon (the first time since the early 2000s). 
•  Through late March and April 2020, stations in multiple states (including Kentucky, Wisconsin, Michigan, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi, Missouri, Ohio, and others) offered gas under $1, with some reports as low as around 89 cents. 
This was driven by the sharp drop in driving demand from COVID lockdowns, plus an oil price war between Saudi Arabia and Russia. Around the same time (April 20, 2020), WTI crude oil futures briefly went negative (settling at about –$37.63 per barrel) due to storage constraints—not a typical retail “per gallon” price. 
National averages stayed above $1 the entire period; the sub-$1 prices were local/station-specific.

text:
This is one of my favorite Dolly stories, because it's basically a masterclass disguised as a sweet little anecdote.

Elvis wants to record "I Will Always Love You." Dolly wrote it. Dreams come true, right?

Then Colonel Parker steps in and says, sure, but we want a cut of the publishing. Dolly owned that song outright. Giving part of it away, even for Elvis, even for a moment like that, wasn't something she'd do.

She said no. Heartbroken about it, by her own account. But she held the line.

Years later, Whitney Houston records it for The Bodyguard, and it becomes one of the biggest songs of all time. Dolly's joked since that the royalties from that one version alone basically paid for Graceland.

Knowing what you can't afford to give away, even when the offer in front of you is Elvis Presley himself, that's the real lesson hiding in that story.

text:
here’s a summary, because i don’t have time to go into all the details. if you have questions let me know.

The case against consummation starts with the sources. Every claim of sexual contact is late, secondhand, and hostile. McLellin's barn story surfaced in 1872, more than 35 years after the events. He said he had heard the story, and he claimed Emma confirmed it in 1847, yet there is no record of Emma ever acknowledging that Joseph practiced polygamy. The pregnancy claim traces to Chauncey Webb, filtered through an anti-Mormon writer in 1886. Webb was in a position to know about a pregnancy but offered no further details, and the supposed scandal didn't stop him from following Joseph to Nauvoo and the Saints to Utah. No child has ever been identified, and Fanny married Solomon Custer in November 1836 without any recorded scandal attached to her.

The other evidence fits a non-sexual reading —Oliver opposed polygamy on principle, so "dirty, nasty, filthy" could reflect disgust at a plural sealing itself, not proof of sex, and the letterbook's original word may have been the vaguer "scrape." Joseph's position at the time was that the relationship was not adulterous, which is compatible with a ceremony that was never physically completed. Some researchers propose a different kind of bond altogether, pointing to Eliza Jane Churchill Webb's description of Fanny as an "adopted daughter" of the Smiths, whose mother claimed she was sealed to Joseph at the time of adoption. That reading would explain why the Alger family stayed proud of the connection. None of this proves there was no sexual relationship, but the evidence that there was one is weak enough that it remains an open question.

I.e we simply don’t have enough reason to say it was consummated. can we say it equally wasn’t? no, but the truth on the matter is that neither of us know except God, Joseph and Fanny.

#Navratri | A stone-carved story of Shakti, centuries old.

At Aihole in Karnataka, the Durga Temple preserves some of the finest examples of Early Chalukyan sculpture. Dating to around the 6th century CE, the temple belongs to a period when Aihole was emerging as an important centre of Indian temple architecture and artistic experimentation.

Among the temple’s sculptural traditions is Mahishamardini - the Goddess as the slayer of Mahishasura, a powerful form of Durga and Shakti in Indian art and religious imagination.

As Sharad Navratri begins, this ancient sculpture offers a glimpse into how the story and imagery of the Goddess have lived through India’s artistic heritage across centuries.

From Early Chalukyan art to living Navratri traditions, the story of Shakti continues to be remembered, celebrated and reimagined.

Bharat Ki Soch wishes you a Shubh Navratri filled with strength, knowledge and auspicious beginnings.

Like my family has always belived in the interconnectedness of things 

Forced conversion to Christianity has occurred in multiple historical periods and regions, though official church doctrine often formally opposed pure coercion while practice frequently diverged. The topic connects directly to the X post we discussed earlier, in which the author referenced Jewish family ancestry involving forced conversion.

In the context of Jewish communities, documented episodes include:

- Early medieval waves in Visigothic Spain, parts of the Byzantine Empire, Gaul, and Italy, sometimes under royal decrees requiring baptism or expulsion.
- Crusader-related violence in the Rhineland (1096) and elsewhere, where Jews faced the choice of conversion or death during mob attacks.
- Large-scale events in Spain after the 1391 pogroms, in which many Jews converted under threat of violence; the 1492 Alhambra Decree then offered remaining Jews the choice of conversion or expulsion, while Portugal in 1496–97 carried out mass forced baptisms of nearly its entire Jewish population. Descendants of these converts (conversos or New Christians) were later targeted by the Spanish Inquisition for suspected crypto-Judaism.[](<https://t.co/3sX1Q2XlGA>)

Official Catholic teaching, reflected in the Fourth Council of Toledo (633), Gratian’s Decretum, and later figures such as Thomas Aquinas, generally held that Jews should not be forcibly baptized because genuine faith requires free will. Papal protections (such as the Constitutio pro Judaeis) repeatedly prohibited violence aimed at forcing baptism. In practice, however, local rulers, mobs, economic pressures, mandatory conversion sermons, and the rule that a baptism once performed could not be renounced created coercive environments. Once baptized under duress, individuals and their descendants were often treated as Christians who could be punished for returning to Judaism.[](<https://t.co/3sX1Q2XlGA>)

Broader historical patterns also included military and colonial coercion directed at non-Jewish groups. Charlemagne’s campaigns against the Saxons and later Baltic crusades involved forced conversion of pagans. In Spanish America, mass baptisms of Indigenous peoples occurred alongside colonial power structures, the Requerimiento, and campaigns against “idolatry,” though Indians were often under different legal jurisdictions from the Inquisition and syncretic practices remained common.

“Forced” covers a spectrum ranging from immediate threat of death or violence to sustained legal disabilities, social exclusion, and economic pressure. Voluntary conversions also took place throughout Christian history. Comparative histories note that coercive conversion policies have appeared under other religious regimes as well, including certain periods of Islamic rule in Iberia and elsewhere. In modern times, major Christian bodies (especially the Catholic Church after Vatican II) have largely rejected targeted proselytism of Jews and acknowledged the historical record of coercion and persecution.

These episodes left long-term effects, including crypto-Jewish communities that preserved elements of Jewish practice in secret for generations, as well as ongoing scholarly and communal discussion of identity, ancestry, and religious freedom.
